flashcards.back: Forest-wide (one per forest): Schema Master, Domain Naming Master. Domain-wide (one per domain): RID Master, PDC Emulator, Infrastructure Master.
flashcards.detail: PDC Emulator handles time sync and password-change urgency; Infrastructure Master fixes cross-domain group-membership references and should NOT sit on a Global Catalog server unless every DC in the domain is also a GC.

flashcards.back: Intra-site replication is frequent (change-notification triggered) and uncompressed, using a ring topology built automatically by the Knowledge Consistency Checker (KCC). Inter-site replication runs on a schedule over site links, compressed to save WAN bandwidth.
flashcards.detail: A site link's cost and replication interval control how the KCC builds the inter-site spanning tree — lower cost is preferred, and bridgehead servers are the DCs that actually replicate across the link.

flashcards.back: A forest trust is transitive between two entire forests. An external trust is non-transitive, linking two specific domains (often across forests). A shortcut trust shortens the referral path between two domains deep in the same forest. A realm trust connects a domain to a non-Windows Kerberos realm.
flashcards.detail: Transitive doesn't mean unlimited — a forest trust does not automatically extend to a third forest that one of the two trusted forests trusts.

flashcards.front: Group Policy processing order and precedence
flashcards.back: GPOs apply in the order Local, Site, Domain, OU (LSDOU), with the last one applied — the OU closest to the object — normally winning a conflict. 'Enforced' on a GPO overrides that and always wins, even against Block Inheritance on a child OU.
flashcards.detail: Block Inheritance stops higher-level GPOs from applying to an OU, but it cannot stop a GPO explicitly marked Enforced — enforcement beats blocking.

flashcards.back: Password Hash Synchronization (PHS) syncs a hash of the password hash to Microsoft Entra ID so sign-in works even if on-premises AD is down. Pass-through Authentication (PTA) validates the password against on-premises AD in real time via an agent, keeping the actual validation on-premises. Federation (AD FS) delegates authentication entirely to an on-premises federation service.
flashcards.detail: PHS never transmits a recoverable, plaintext password to the cloud — only a hash of the hash — which is a common exam misconception to watch for.

flashcards.back: An RODC holds a read-only copy of the AD database, ideal for branch offices with weaker physical security. It caches credentials only for accounts allowed by its Password Replication Policy (PRP), and it holds a filtered attribute set that excludes sensitive data.
flashcards.detail: If an RODC is compromised, only the passwords it was permitted to cache are at risk — not the whole domain's credentials — which is the entire point of the PRP.

flashcards.front: AD Recycle Bin vs. tombstone reanimation
flashcards.back: The AD Recycle Bin (available once forest functional level is Windows Server 2008 R2 or higher and the feature is enabled) restores a deleted object with essentially all of its original attributes, including group memberships. Tombstone reanimation, the older method, recovers a bare object that has lost most of its link-valued attributes.
flashcards.detail: Enabling the AD Recycle Bin is a one-way, irreversible action for the forest — a detail the exam likes to test.

flashcards.back: A gMSA provides one identity that multiple servers (like a load-balanced web farm) can use for a service, with automatic password rotation managed by AD — no manual password management or synchronization needed across servers.
flashcards.detail: A standalone (single-server) MSA cannot be shared across multiple hosts — only a gMSA can, because only a gMSA replicates its managed password data through AD to every authorized host.

flashcards.back: A GC server holds a full, writable copy of its own domain plus a partial, read-only copy of every other domain in the forest, enabling forest-wide searches and universal group membership resolution during logon.
flashcards.detail: Without a reachable GC, a user in a multi-domain forest logging on with a UPN, or one belonging to a universal group, can be blocked from completing logon — universal group membership can only be resolved via the GC.

flashcards.back: Azure Arc projects an on-premises (or other-cloud) server into Azure Resource Manager as an Arc-enabled resource via the Connected Machine agent, without migrating the actual workload. Once projected, you can apply Azure Policy, Azure Monitor, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, and Update Manager to it just like a native Azure VM.
flashcards.detail: Arc gives you Azure's management plane over a server that never leaves your datacenter — the compute itself stays exactly where it is.

flashcards.back: A free, browser-based management tool for Windows Server (and Windows client), installed as a gateway on a management PC/server or as a service, giving a modern portal-style UI for managing local or remote servers including Server Core.
flashcards.detail: WAC extends with feature extensions (like Azure Arc integration) but runs entirely from a browser — no separate console application to install on every admin's workstation.

flashcards.back: Automates installing Windows updates across every node in a failover cluster one at a time, draining (moving) that node's workloads to other nodes before patching and rebooting it, then bringing it back before moving to the next node.
flashcards.detail: CAU can run against a remote CAU-enabled cluster on a schedule, with no dedicated CAU role required on the cluster itself, or in a self-updating mode where the cluster updates itself.

flashcards.back: Asynchronously replicates a running VM's changes from a primary Hyper-V host to a replica host (on-premises or another site), on a configurable interval as low as 30 seconds, keeping extra recovery points and supporting a manual, planned, or unplanned failover.
flashcards.detail: Hyper-V Replica does not require Failover Clustering or shared storage at all — it works between two standalone Hyper-V hosts, which is a common exam distinction from clustered, S2D-based high availability.

flashcards.back: Migrates files, shares, and their security and configuration from an old file server (or cluster) to a new one, and can optionally transfer the old server's identity (name and IP address) to the new server afterward, so clients keep using the same UNC path with no reconfiguration.
flashcards.detail: It uses three roles — an orchestrator, a source server, and a destination server — and can inventory and migrate from Windows Server as far back as Windows Server 2003, and even from some NAS devices, not only recent Windows Server versions.

flashcards.front: Failover cluster quorum models and witness types
flashcards.back: A cluster stays online only while a majority of its votes are present. Node Majority gives one vote per node (best for an odd node count). Node and File Share Majority and Node and Disk Majority add one extra vote from a witness (a file share or a shared disk) so an even node count can still form a majority. Cloud Witness uses Azure Blob Storage as that witness instead, avoiding a second physical site.
flashcards.detail: Cloud Witness is the common exam-favorite pick for a two-node hybrid cluster with no convenient third site to host a traditional file-share witness — it needs only a small Azure Storage account, not a full VM or site.

flashcards.back: A wizard-driven or PowerShell-driven suite of tests (Test-Cluster) checking that nodes, storage, and networking meet Microsoft's requirements before a cluster is created, and useful again after changes to confirm the cluster still meets them.
flashcards.detail: Running validation is a prerequisite for a Microsoft-supported cluster — a cluster built while skipping or failing validation is explicitly called out as unsupported if a validation-related issue later causes an outage.

flashcards.back: External: binds to a physical NIC, giving VMs access to the physical network (and the host, if allowed). Internal: lets VMs and the host communicate with each other, but not the physical network. Private: lets VMs on the same host communicate with each other only, isolated even from the host.
flashcards.detail: A private switch is the right call for an isolated test/lab network where VMs must talk to each other but must never reach the production network or even the host OS.

flashcards.back: Generation 1 VMs emulate legacy BIOS hardware and boot from IDE/legacy devices, for maximum OS compatibility. Generation 2 VMs use UEFI firmware, support Secure Boot, and boot directly from SCSI, offering better performance and security features but requiring a 64-bit, UEFI-aware guest OS.
flashcards.detail: Once created, a VM's generation cannot be changed — choosing wrong means recreating the VM rather than converting it in place.

flashcards.back: A standard checkpoint captures the VM's memory and device state, like a saved game — fast, but not application-aware. A production checkpoint uses Volume Shadow Copy Service (VSS) inside the guest to create an application-consistent point-in-time copy, safe to use against things like SQL Server or Active Directory.
flashcards.detail: Only production checkpoints are safe as a routine 'backup-like' snapshot of a database or domain controller VM — a standard checkpoint's crash-consistent state can cause serious problems if restored into a running DC.

flashcards.front: Live Migration vs. Storage Migration vs. Hyper-V Replica
flashcards.back: Live Migration moves a running VM between Hyper-V hosts with no downtime, needing shared/replicated storage (or SMB 3.0) and compatible processors (or Processor Compatibility Mode). Storage Migration moves a VM's virtual disks to different storage with no downtime, without changing hosts. Hyper-V Replica asynchronously replicates a VM to a secondary host/site for disaster recovery, not for routine load balancing.
flashcards.detail: Hyper-V Replica is a DR tool, not a live-migration substitute — its replica VM sits offline until you actually fail over to it.

flashcards.front: Windows container isolation: process vs. Hyper-V
flashcards.back: Process-isolated containers share the host's kernel directly, giving the lowest overhead but weaker isolation between containers. Hyper-V isolated containers each run inside their own lightweight utility VM with its own kernel instance, trading some overhead for stronger, VM-grade isolation.
flashcards.detail: Hyper-V isolation is the choice for running containers from mutually distrusting tenants on the same host, or when the container's base image doesn't exactly match the host's kernel version.

flashcards.back: A primary zone holds the writable, authoritative copy of a zone. A secondary zone holds a read-only copy transferred (via zone transfer) from a primary. A stub zone holds only NS, SOA, and glue A/AAAA records — enough to find the authoritative servers, not the full record set. An AD-integrated zone stores its data in Active Directory for automatic multi-master replication and secure dynamic updates.
flashcards.detail: A stub zone is much lighter than a secondary zone precisely because it only tracks who is authoritative for a namespace, not the records themselves — it's a referral shortcut, not a resolvable copy.

flashcards.front: DHCP failover: load balance vs. hot standby
flashcards.back: Load balance mode has both DHCP servers actively answering client requests, splitting the load by a configured percentage. Hot standby mode has one server active and one passive backup that only starts answering if the active server becomes unavailable.
flashcards.detail: Hot standby is the natural fit for a branch office scenario, where a central DHCP server normally handles everything and a local server only takes over if the WAN link to the central site drops.

flashcards.back: IPAM is a Windows Server role that discovers, monitors, and centrally manages DHCP and DNS servers and their IP address space from one console, including tracking utilization and flagging overlapping or duplicate scopes across the environment.
flashcards.detail: IPAM manages existing DHCP/DNS server roles — it isn't itself a DHCP or DNS server, and installing it doesn't remove the need to also deploy those roles somewhere.

flashcards.back: A site-to-site VPN connects on-premises networks to Azure over the public internet using encrypted tunnels — cheaper and quicker to stand up, but subject to internet variability. ExpressRoute uses a private, dedicated circuit provisioned through a connectivity provider, bypassing the public internet for more predictable latency, higher available bandwidth, and higher cost.
flashcards.detail: ExpressRoute traffic doesn't traverse the public internet at all, which is also why it's commonly paired with a VPN as an encrypted backup path in case the ExpressRoute circuit itself fails.

flashcards.back: NPS is Microsoft's RADIUS server and proxy implementation, centralizing authentication, authorization, and accounting for things like VPN connections, 802.1X wired/wireless access, and other RADIUS-aware network devices.
flashcards.detail: NPS itself doesn't terminate the VPN connection — RRAS (or a third-party VPN device) does that and forwards the authentication request to NPS as the RADIUS server.

flashcards.back: DFS Namespaces (DFS-N) presents a single logical folder path (like \\contoso\shares) that transparently points to shared folders on one or more servers. DFS Replication (DFS-R) keeps the actual folder contents synchronized between multiple servers so any of them can serve current data.
flashcards.detail: They're commonly used together — DFS-R keeps the copies in sync, while DFS-N gives users one path that resolves to whichever in-sync copy is closest or available — but each can be deployed independently of the other. Storage Replica solves a related but block-level replication problem, not a file-share one.

flashcards.back: Simple striping spreads data with no redundancy (fastest, no fault tolerance). A two-way (or three-way) mirror duplicates data across disks, tolerating one (or two) disk failures with strong write performance. Parity spreads data plus parity information, more storage-efficient than mirroring for the same fault tolerance, but with slower random writes.
flashcards.detail: Parity's storage efficiency comes at a real performance cost on writes — it's a better fit for larger, less write-intensive data like backups or archives than for a busy transactional workload.

flashcards.back: S2D pools local, direct-attached storage (typically SATA/NVMe/SAS disks) across the nodes of a failover cluster into a single software-defined storage pool, enabling hyperconverged infrastructure without a separate SAN.
flashcards.detail: S2D requires a functioning failover cluster underneath it — it's a storage feature built on top of clustering, not a replacement for it, so failover cluster quorum models and witness types still apply to it.

flashcards.back: A post-process, file-system-level feature (on volumes, not the OS volume by default) that finds and eliminates duplicate chunks of data on disk, replacing repeats with references to a single stored copy. It fits general file shares, VDI libraries, and backup targets well.
flashcards.detail: Deduplication is a poor fit for heavily and randomly modified files like live database (.mdf) files or files already compressed/encrypted, where duplicate chunks are rare or the savings aren't worth the processing overhead.

flashcards.back: Azure File Sync keeps an on-premises Windows Server file share in sync with an Azure file share, and can enable cloud tiering — infrequently used files are replaced locally with a pointer while their full content stays safely in Azure, streamed back on access.
flashcards.detail: Cloud tiering means the local server's disk shows the full namespace even though cold files' actual bytes have been evicted locally — from a user's perspective the file is still just 'there,' just retrieved on demand.

flashcards.back: ReFS (Resilient File System) prioritizes resiliency and scalability for large data volumes, using checksums and automatic corruption repair (with mirrored/parity Storage Spaces) and integrating tightly with features like block cloning. NTFS remains the general-purpose default and is required for the Windows Server boot/system volume.
flashcards.detail: ReFS is not supported as a boot volume for Windows Server — it's meant for data volumes, particularly ones backed by Storage Spaces where its self-healing features can actually repair detected corruption.

flashcards.back: Storage Replica provides block-level, volume-to-volume replication between servers or clusters, independent of the file system on top. Synchronous replication guarantees zero data loss but requires low latency between sites; asynchronous replication tolerates higher latency at the cost of a small, non-zero possible data loss window.
flashcards.detail: Because it replicates at the block level below the file system, Storage Replica works for any workload on the volume — it doesn't care whether the data is SQL files, general shares, or anything else.

flashcards.front: Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) vs. AppLocker
flashcards.back: WDAC enforces a code-integrity policy that determines what is allowed to run before it starts, evaluated by the kernel itself and applied system-wide. AppLocker is a rule-based allowlisting feature that runs at the user-mode level and can apply different rules per user or group, but is easier to bypass than WDAC.
flashcards.detail: WDAC policies can run in enforced or audit mode, and unlike AppLocker, a WDAC policy applies before a user even logs on, since it is enforced by the kernel rather than a user-mode service.

flashcards.back: Uses virtualization-based security (VBS) to isolate the LSASS process and NTLM/Kerberos secrets inside a protected, hypervisor-enforced container, so that even an administrator on the host, or malware with kernel-level access, cannot extract them with tools like Mimikatz.
flashcards.detail: Credential Guard requires hardware virtualization support (Hyper-V, SLAT, a compatible processor) and blocks storing reversibly-encrypted passwords and unconstrained Kerberos delegation, which is a common reason it breaks specific legacy authentication scenarios.

flashcards.back: Automatically rotates and stores the password for a local administrator account on each domain-joined (or Microsoft Entra-joined) computer, either in Active Directory or Microsoft Entra ID, with access controlled by delegated permissions.
flashcards.detail: Windows LAPS is built into modern Windows Server and Windows client and can back up a managed account's passphrase history, replacing the older, separately-installed LAPS tool.

flashcards.back: Adding an account to the Protected Users group blocks it from authenticating with NTLM, DES, or RC4 encryption, prevents credential caching, and disables delegation of its credentials, forcing Kerberos with stronger encryption only.
flashcards.detail: It is a strong control for high-privilege accounts, but it is unforgiving: an application or device that only supports NTLM will simply fail to authenticate that account, with no fallback available.

flashcards.back: A cloud service that monitors on-premises AD DS, via sensors installed on domain controllers, for signs of compromise such as reconnaissance, pass-the-hash, DCSync attempts, or golden ticket usage, surfacing those alerts alongside other Microsoft Defender XDR signals.
flashcards.detail: Unlike Entra ID Identity Protection, which focuses on cloud sign-ins, Defender for Identity is specifically about detecting attacks against the on-premises identity plane itself.

flashcards.front: Performance Monitor and Data Collector Sets
flashcards.back: Performance Monitor displays real-time or logged performance counters (like CPU, memory, disk queue length). A Data Collector Set groups counters, trace data, and configuration into a single, reusable, schedulable collection job, so the same set of metrics can be captured consistently over time rather than configured freshly each time.
flashcards.detail: A Data Collector Set can be configured to trigger an alert, or run a task, when a counter crosses a defined threshold, which is what turns raw performance data into a proactive monitoring signal instead of a report someone has to read manually.

flashcards.front: Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) and Data Collection Rules (DCR)
flashcards.back: AMA is the unified agent installed on Azure VMs, Arc-enabled servers, or other machines to collect logs and performance data. A Data Collection Rule defines exactly what that agent collects, any transformation applied, and which Log Analytics workspace (or other destination) it is sent to.
flashcards.detail: AMA replaces the older Log Analytics (MMA/OMS) agent, and one DCR can be associated with many machines, which is what lets a single collection configuration apply consistently across a whole hybrid fleet.

flashcards.front: Log Analytics workspace and Kusto Query Language (KQL)
flashcards.back: A Log Analytics workspace is the container where Azure Monitor stores collected log data, queried using KQL, a read-only query language built around piping data through a chain of operators (like where, summarize, and project) to filter and shape results.
flashcards.detail: Workspace-based queries also power log alert rules, so a KQL query that flags a problem interactively can usually be turned directly into an automated alert with very little extra work.

flashcards.front: Azure Monitor alert rules and action groups
flashcards.back: A metric alert evaluates a numeric signal (like CPU percentage) against a threshold on a schedule. A log alert runs a KQL query on a schedule and fires based on its results. An action group defines what happens when either fires — for example, an email, an SMS, a webhook, or an Azure Automation runbook.
flashcards.detail: Separating the alert rule (the condition) from the action group (the response) means the same action group, say, paging the on-call team, can be reused across many different, unrelated alert rules.

flashcards.front: Windows Admin Center monitoring and alerts
flashcards.back: Windows Admin Center shows real-time and historical performance data for a managed server directly in the browser, and its Azure Monitor extension can forward that data to Log Analytics and configure alert rules from the same interface, without switching to the Azure portal.
flashcards.detail: This lets an admin manage a purely on-premises server's health with the same tool used for day-to-day administration, while still optionally layering on Azure-based alerting for it.

flashcards.back: Centrally assesses update compliance and schedules update installation across Azure VMs and Azure Arc-enabled on-premises (or other-cloud) servers from one place in the Azure portal, replacing the need to manage separate on-premises patching tools for those machines.
flashcards.detail: A server must be Arc-enabled, or be a native Azure VM, before Update Manager can see or patch it at all — a plain on-premises server with no Arc agent and no Azure connection is invisible to it.

flashcards.front: Reliability Monitor and Event Viewer for troubleshooting
flashcards.back: Reliability Monitor plots a rolling stability index over time and correlates it with specific events (installs, crashes, updates), making it easy to spot when a problem started. Event Viewer provides the full, detailed event logs (System, Application, Security, and role-specific logs) needed to diagnose exactly what happened at that point.
flashcards.detail: Reliability Monitor is a good first stop for figuring out when something started going wrong, after which Event Viewer's more detailed, filterable logs are what actually confirm the root cause.

flashcards.back: Password Settings Objects let different password and lockout rules apply to specific users or groups within one domain, instead of the single domain-wide default policy applying to everyone equally.
flashcards.detail: A requirement for service accounts to follow a stricter, separate password policy than regular users — without splitting them into another domain — is exactly the scenario PSOs solve, often paired with Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) for the accounts themselves.

flashcards.back: A minimal Windows Server install with no desktop shell or most GUI tools, managed remotely via PowerShell, Windows Admin Center, or Server Manager — reducing the attack surface, patching footprint, and resource use compared to Desktop Experience.
flashcards.detail: Server Core is commonly managed day-to-day through Windows Admin Center (WAC) precisely because there's no local desktop shell to open management consoles from directly.

flashcards.back: A setting that gates which AD DS features are available, based on the oldest domain controller OS version the domain (or forest) must still support — raising the level unlocks newer features but permanently rules out adding an older-OS domain controller afterward.
flashcards.detail: This is why a domain controller upgrade project often plans to retire the oldest DCs first — the functional level can't go up while an old one is still present, and it can't come back down once raised.

flashcards.back: A Windows Server role that presents block-level storage over the network as an iSCSI target, letting a client (physical or virtual) connect to it as if it were a local disk — a software-defined alternative to a dedicated SAN.
flashcards.detail: This is a different sharing model than DFS Namespaces vs. DFS Replication, which share file-level folders — iSCSI instead hands over a raw block device the client formats and manages itself.

flashcards.front: Group Policy Preferences vs. Group Policy settings
flashcards.back: Group Policy settings are enforced and grayed out for the end user, reapplied continuously. Group Policy Preferences configure an initial value (like a mapped drive or a desktop shortcut) that the user can subsequently change, and aren't strictly re-enforced the same way.
flashcards.detail: This distinction — enforced vs. merely pre-configured — is a common exam trap, since both live in the same Group Policy Management Console and both flow through Group Policy processing order and precedence.

flashcards.back: Always On VPN is Microsoft's modern client-access VPN, automatically connecting a Windows device to the corporate network whenever it's off-network and replacing the discontinued DirectAccess. It solves a different connectivity problem than Site-to-Site VPN vs. ExpressRoute, which link two entire networks together — Always On VPN instead connects one remote device at a time, and commonly authenticates through Network Policy Server (NPS) as its RADIUS backend, the same way a traditional RRAS-terminated VPN would.
flashcards.detail: Always On VPN supports a device tunnel that connects automatically before user sign-in, alongside a separate user tunnel established after sign-in, which is what lets IT reach and manage a laptop over the VPN even before anyone has logged on to it.

flashcards.back: A conditional forwarder tells a DNS server to forward queries for one specific namespace to a specific list of DNS servers, rather than resolving them itself — a simpler, lower-maintenance alternative to hosting a stub zone (one of the DNS zone types) when all that's needed is a forwarding rule, not a locally cached set of NS/SOA/glue records for that namespace.
flashcards.detail: Unlike a stub zone, a conditional forwarder keeps no local copy of records at all — if the target DNS servers become unreachable, queries for that namespace simply fail rather than falling back to a stale, locally cached referral.

flashcards.back: WSUS is the traditional on-premises role for approving, staging, and distributing Windows updates to domain-joined clients and servers from local infrastructure, entirely independent of any Azure connection. It doesn't get replaced by Azure Update Manager the moment a server is Arc-enabled — the two can run side by side, and Update Manager specifically needs to be enabled for a server on top of Arc enrollment before it reports or manages that server's patch compliance at all.
flashcards.detail: A common exam trap is assuming Arc-enabling a server automatically hands its patch management to Update Manager — being Arc-enabled alone doesn't start update compliance reporting; Update Manager still has to be explicitly enabled for that specific machine.

flashcards.back: BitLocker encrypts an entire volume at rest, typically sealed to a TPM chip so the drive only unlocks on its original hardware, with recovery keys escrowed to AD DS or Microsoft Entra ID rather than left only on the local machine. It protects a very different attack surface than Credential Guard, which isolates secrets already in memory on a running system — a stolen, powered-off drive is exactly what BitLocker defends, while a compromised, powered-on server still needs Credential Guard to keep an attacker from lifting credentials out of LSASS. For local administrator passwords specifically, Windows LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) plays the analogous escrow role, rotating and storing a password so it's never only kept on one device.
flashcards.detail: BitLocker requires a TPM (or a USB startup key as a workaround) and, like Credential Guard, needs hardware virtualization or platform security features that a very old or virtualized-without-vTPM machine may not actually offer.

flashcards.front: Authoritative vs. non-authoritative restore (Directory Services Restore Mode)
flashcards.back: A non-authoritative restore replays a backed-up domain controller's database and then lets normal replication catch it back up with any changes its partners made since the backup. An authoritative restore (performed with ntdsutil after booting into Directory Services Restore Mode, DSRM) instead marks specific restored objects as the ones to push out to every other domain controller, overwriting the newer changes — including an unwanted deletion — those DCs already hold.
flashcards.detail: DSRM is a special boot mode that starts a domain controller without AD DS running, unlocked with the separate DSRM administrator password set at promotion — a password many admins forget exists until the moment they actually need it.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Entra Domain Services (Microsoft Entra DS)
flashcards.back: A fully managed service that stands up a traditional, domain-joinable AD DS domain in Azure — complete with Kerberos/NTLM authentication and Group Policy — without deploying or patching any domain controllers yourself. It's a separate, one-way-synced domain from on-premises AD, not the same thing as Microsoft Entra Connect authentication methods, which instead synchronize identities into Entra ID itself rather than creating a whole managed domain.
flashcards.detail: A frequent exam distinction: Microsoft Entra Connect synchronizes identity objects into Microsoft Entra ID for cloud sign-in, while Microsoft Entra Domain Services gives you an actual managed, domain-joinable AD DS environment in Azure for legacy apps that need traditional domain membership — they solve different problems and are often used together.

flashcards.back: A cluster set groups multiple separate failover clusters into one larger software-defined compute and storage fabric, letting VMs live-migrate across the member clusters' boundaries for far greater scale than any single cluster supports, while each member cluster keeps its own failover cluster quorum models and witness types.
flashcards.detail: Think of a cluster set as a 'cluster of clusters' — it's aimed at hyperscale or hosting-provider deployments that have outgrown a single cluster's node-count ceiling, not a typical mid-size organization's first failover cluster.

flashcards.back: Extended replication adds a third copy of a VM on top of an ordinary Hyper-V Replica pair, replicating asynchronously from the existing replica host to a second replica host, often at a third site, so a single-site failure doesn't also take out the only remaining disaster-recovery copy.
flashcards.detail: Extended replication layers on top of an already-working primary-to-replica relationship — it isn't a replacement for that pair, just an additional safety net configured once the first replica is already running.

flashcards.back: NAT mode (Docker's default on Windows) gives each container a private IP behind address translation on the host. Transparent mode connects a container directly to the physical network, appearing as its own host on the LAN. L2Bridge mode shares the host's IP subnet with containers using their own MAC address. Overlay mode spans multiple hosts for container-to-container networking across a cluster, typically with Docker Swarm.
flashcards.detail: Network mode choice is independent of isolation mode — see Process isolation and container base image compatibility for the separate build-matching constraint that applies only to process-isolated containers.

flashcards.front: Shielded virtual machines and Host Guardian Service (HGS)
flashcards.back: A shielded VM encrypts its virtual disk and state with BitLocker and limits even fabric (host/hypervisor) administrators from inspecting it, console-connecting to it, or extracting its keys. The Host Guardian Service attests that a Hyper-V host is healthy and trusted before releasing the key needed to run that shielded VM, using either hardware-based TPM-trusted attestation or the weaker admin-trusted attestation.
flashcards.detail: This defends against a threat Credential Guard doesn't cover: Credential Guard isolates secrets on one already-running machine, while shielded VMs stop a compromised or malicious fabric administrator with full host console access from reading a tenant VM's memory or disk at all.

flashcards.front: Process isolation and container base image compatibility
flashcards.back: A process-isolated Windows container shares the host's kernel directly, so its base container image build must match (or be compatible with) the host OS build — a mismatch simply fails to start the container. Hyper-V isolation avoids this constraint entirely, since each container runs its own kernel inside a lightweight utility VM.
flashcards.detail: This build-matching requirement is a frequent real-world container deployment failure on Windows Server — an image built against a newer Windows Server base often won't run process-isolated on an older host build, which is exactly when switching to Hyper-V isolation becomes the fix.

flashcards.back: A Windows Admin Center feature that automatically provisions a point-to-site VPN connection from an on-premises server straight into an Azure virtual network, without manually configuring RRAS, certificates, or a VPN gateway by hand.
flashcards.detail: It's a quick way to reach Azure VNet resources from a single on-premises server for testing or a small workload — for connecting entire networks together at scale, a Site-to-Site VPN vs. ExpressRoute decision is still the right call instead.

flashcards.back: A Windows Server role that turns a server into a software router, NAT device, and VPN termination point — handling site-to-site and point-to-site VPN connections, legacy DirectAccess infrastructure, and basic LAN/WAN routing, all from one role.
flashcards.detail: RRAS is the piece that actually terminates a VPN connection and forwards the authentication request onward to Network Policy Server (NPS) as the RADIUS server — RRAS and NPS are commonly deployed together but are not the same role.

flashcards.front: File Server Resource Manager (FSRM) quotas and file screening
flashcards.back: FSRM lets an administrator cap how much data a user or folder can store (quotas, as either a hard limit or a soft warning-only limit) and block specific file types from being saved to a share (file screening), plus generate storage reports — all without touching NTFS permissions.
flashcards.detail: A quota and a file screen solve different problems: a quota limits total space regardless of file type, while a file screen blocks specific file types, like .mp3 or .exe, regardless of how much space is left.

flashcards.back: A clustered file server role, built on Cluster Shared Volumes, where every cluster node can serve the same SMB shares simultaneously and actively — unlike a traditional clustered general-use file server, where only one node owns a given share at a time.
flashcards.detail: SOFS is the typical front end for Hyper-V-over-SMB or Storage Spaces Direct (S2D)-backed storage, since active-active access across every node avoids the slower failover of a traditional file server share moving between nodes one at a time.

flashcards.back: A PowerShell-based constrained administration feature that limits a connecting user to a specific, defined set of cmdlets, parameters, and values (via a role capability file), running those operations under a virtual account behind the scenes — so a support technician can perform specific tasks without ever receiving full local administrator rights.
flashcards.detail: JEA solves a different problem than Windows LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution): LAPS manages and rotates an actual local administrator password, while JEA avoids handing out administrator rights at all by constraining exactly what a non-administrator session is allowed to run.

flashcards.front: Authentication policies and authentication policy silos
flashcards.back: An authentication policy restricts how a specific account, typically a high-privilege one, is allowed to authenticate — for example, only from specific domain controllers or devices — and can set a stricter Kerberos ticket lifetime for it. An authentication policy silo groups related accounts and the devices or servers they're allowed to touch into one boundary, so a compromised low-value account can't be used to reach high-value servers outside that silo.
flashcards.detail: This pairs naturally with the Protected Users security group — Protected Users forces stronger Kerberos-only authentication for an account, while an authentication policy silo additionally restricts which specific machines that account can even attempt to sign in to or from.

flashcards.back: A built-in Windows feature that centralizes selected event log entries from many source servers onto one collector server, using a WinRM-based subscription — no Azure agent, Log Analytics workspace, or extra licensing required.
flashcards.detail: WEF is the right call when a scenario specifically rules out Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) and Data Collection Rules (DCR) and still wants centralized Security/Application log review using only built-in Windows Server functionality.

flashcards.front: VM insights and the dependency map
flashcards.back: VM insights, built on Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) and Data Collection Rules (DCR) plus a separate Dependency Agent, shows a server's running processes and the discovered connections and dependencies between servers — useful for migration planning and tracing a cross-server issue, across both Azure VMs and Arc-enabled on-premises servers.
flashcards.detail: The dependency map is what actually visualizes those discovered connections between machines — AMA alone collects logs and performance counters, but it's the separate Dependency Agent that supplies the process- and connection-level data the map is built from.

flashcards.front: AD FS and Web Application Proxy (WAP)
flashcards.back: AD FS issues claims-based security tokens so users can single sign-on to relying-party applications (including many SaaS apps) using their on-premises AD credentials, as the Federation option among Microsoft Entra Connect authentication methods. Web Application Proxy (WAP) sits in the perimeter network and relays those federation requests to the internal AD FS farm, so the AD FS servers themselves never have to be placed directly in, or reachable from, the perimeter network.
flashcards.detail: WAP also pre-authenticates and publishes other internal web applications to external users, not just AD FS traffic, but publishing AD FS is its most common AZ-802 scenario.

flashcards.front: Group Policy troubleshooting: RSoP, gpresult, and gpupdate
flashcards.back: gpupdate /force reapplies every GPO to a computer or user immediately instead of waiting for the next background refresh. gpresult /r (or /h for an HTML report) generates a Resultant Set of Policy (RSoP) report showing exactly which GPOs actually applied, and which were filtered out and why, for a specific computer or user. In GPMC, Group Policy Modeling simulates what would apply to a given user/computer/OU combination without needing the target online, while Group Policy Results instead queries a real, already-online target to show what actually applied, including anything decided by Group Policy processing order and precedence.
flashcards.detail: Group Policy Modeling is useful for planning a GPO move before it happens; Group Policy Results (and gpresult) is for confirming what really happened afterward on a live machine.

flashcards.back: Automanage automatically applies, and continuously re-applies if settings drift, a consistent set of Microsoft-recommended best-practice configurations — such as Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Azure Update Manager, Change Tracking and Inventory, and backup — to both native Azure VMs and Azure Arc-enabled servers once they're onboarded, instead of an administrator configuring each of those services by hand on every machine.
flashcards.detail: Automanage builds on top of Azure Arc-enabled servers for non-Azure machines — a server still needs to be Arc-enabled (or be a native Azure VM) before Automanage has anything to manage on it.

flashcards.back: Nested virtualization exposes virtualization extensions from a Hyper-V host down into a running VM, letting that VM itself run Hyper-V (or another hypervisor) and host its own child VMs or containers — useful for a training lab simulating a whole Hyper-V host, or for running tools like Windows Sandbox or WSL2 inside a VM, without needing separate physical hardware per student or scenario.
flashcards.detail: It's enabled per-VM with Set-VMProcessor -ExposeVirtualizationExtensions $true, and requires a processor that supports the needed virtualization extensions on the physical host underneath everything.

flashcards.back: Dynamic Memory lets Hyper-V automatically raise or lower a running VM's assigned memory between a configured minimum and maximum, based on actual demand plus a memory buffer percentage, reclaiming unused memory for other VMs on the host. Static memory instead fixes a VM's memory allocation permanently at one value, which some workloads that manage or tune their own memory internally — such as a SQL Server instance with a carefully sized buffer pool — need, since they don't tolerate their available memory changing underneath them.
flashcards.detail: A VM with Dynamic Memory enabled still needs its maximum set realistically — Hyper-V won't give a VM more memory than the host actually has free to offer, regardless of the configured ceiling.

flashcards.front: Hyper-V VM configuration version and integration services
flashcards.back: Each VM has a configuration version that gates which Hyper-V host features it can use; after moving a VM to a newer Hyper-V host, Update-VMVersion upgrades it to that host's latest supported version — a one-way step that then also prevents moving the VM back to an older host. Integration services, which enable things like Hyper-V enhanced session mode and time synchronization, are now delivered to the guest OS through Windows Update rather than an insertable integration services setup disk.
flashcards.detail: Forgetting that Update-VMVersion is irreversible is a common exam trap — once a VM is upgraded to a newer configuration version, it can no longer live-migrate or move to a host that only supports the older version.

flashcards.front: Switch Embedded Teaming (SET) vs. NIC Teaming
flashcards.back: Switch Embedded Teaming (SET) combines multiple physical NICs into a team directly inside a Hyper-V virtual switch, which is what lets RDMA and Hyper-V's converged networking features keep working on the teamed adapters. Classic NIC Teaming (LBFO) instead teams NICs below any virtual switch, works with a broader range of NIC drivers, but is not compatible with RDMA-capable adapters and can't be combined with SET on the same physical NIC.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario specifically calls for RDMA (for example, SMB Direct for a Scale-Out File Server) on teamed adapters feeding a Hyper-V virtual switch, SET is the only one of the two that supports that combination.

flashcards.back: DNS Policies let a Windows Server DNS server return a different answer to the identical query depending on criteria such as the client's subnet, the time of day, or a server's health, which is useful for directing clients to their closest datacenter or taking a failed site's records out of rotation without editing the zone's actual primary records. Zone scopes are the underlying mechanism — separate, named sets of records inside one zone that a policy chooses between when it decides which answer to return.
flashcards.detail: This is a different tool from a conditional forwarder — a conditional forwarder decides where to send a query for an entire namespace, while a DNS policy decides which stored answer to hand back for a namespace the server already hosts.

flashcards.back: MPIO lets Windows Server use several physical paths — through separate host bus adapters, cables, or switches — to reach the same iSCSI or Fibre Channel storage target, automatically failing over to a surviving path if one drops and, depending on the configured policy, load-balancing I/O across the healthy paths. It solves a storage-path redundancy problem, distinct from what NIC Teaming solves for ordinary network adapters, and often sits underneath a server also connecting to an iSCSI Target Server.
flashcards.detail: MPIO requires the storage target to present the same LUN consistently across every path — Windows uses a device-specific module (DSM) to recognize that multiple paths actually point at one logical disk rather than treating them as separate disks.

flashcards.back: Work Folders syncs a designated folder of a user's files between their devices and a central, on-premises file share (optionally backed by Azure File Sync), so the same personal files stay available and current across a laptop, desktop, and other devices. It's lighter-weight than full Folder Redirection, and access can be constrained with policies like selective wipe of the synced files from a lost or decommissioned device.
flashcards.detail: Work Folders solves a different problem from DFS Namespaces vs. DFS Replication — DFS keeps shared, multi-user folders synchronized between servers, while Work Folders syncs one specific user's own files out to that same user's various devices.

flashcards.front: Storage Spaces thin vs. fixed provisioning
flashcards.back: A fixed-provisioned virtual disk in Storage Spaces immediately reserves its entire configured size from the underlying pool the moment it's created. A thin-provisioned virtual disk instead reports its configured size to the operating system but only consumes actual pool capacity as data is written to it, letting several thin disks share a pool whose physical capacity is smaller than their combined logical size — which requires watching pool capacity over time so it doesn't run out before more physical disks can be added.
flashcards.detail: Thin provisioning trades the convenience of over-allocating disks on paper for an ongoing operational responsibility: letting a thin-provisioned pool silently run out of real capacity is a self-inflicted outage, not a Storage Spaces malfunction.

flashcards.back: AD CS issues and manages digital certificates for a Windows Server environment. An Enterprise CA integrates with AD DS, using certificate templates and Group Policy to support automatic certificate enrollment for users and computers, while a Standalone CA has no AD integration and requires an administrator to manually approve each certificate request. A common deployment pattern is a two-tier hierarchy: an offline root CA that's kept powered down except to issue or revoke subordinate CA certificates, plus an online issuing (subordinate) CA that actually handles day-to-day certificate requests.
flashcards.detail: Keeping the root CA offline means that even if the issuing CA is later compromised, an attacker can't use it to mint a new trusted root — only to have its own certificate revoked and be replaced by a new issuing CA under the same still-trusted root.

flashcards.front: Security Compliance Toolkit and security baselines
flashcards.back: The Security Compliance Toolkit packages Microsoft's own recommended GPO security baseline settings for specific Windows Server and Windows client versions, along with a Policy Analyzer tool to compare baselines (or a live GPO) against each other, and an LGPO tool to import and apply those baseline settings — giving a documented, repeatable starting point for hardening a domain's GPOs instead of building a security-focused GPO's settings from scratch one by one.
flashcards.detail: Because the toolkit ships a specific baseline per OS version, a baseline built for one Windows Server release isn't automatically the right one to apply unmodified to a newer release — it still needs reviewing against the newer version's own published baseline.

flashcards.back: Best Practices Analyzer is a built-in Server Manager tool that scans an installed role, such as AD DS, DHCP, or Hyper-V, against Microsoft's own best-practice configuration rules for that specific role, flagging warnings and non-compliant settings directly in the console — a quick, role-specific health check that needs no Azure agent or external monitoring setup at all.
flashcards.detail: BPA checks a role's own configuration against known-good practice; it doesn't track ongoing performance trends or correlate events the way Performance Monitor and Data Collector Sets or Reliability Monitor and Event Viewer for troubleshooting do.

flashcards.back: Change Tracking and Inventory records software, file, and registry changes made on a server over time, plus an inventory of its installed software and running services, so an administrator can correlate an incident with exactly what changed and when. It's delivered through the same Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) and Data Collection Rule (DCR) already used for other monitoring data, and works for both native Azure VMs and Azure Arc-enabled on-premises servers.
flashcards.detail: This is a natural pairing with Azure Automanage machine configuration, which can enable Change Tracking and Inventory automatically as part of its maintained best-practice configuration set.

questions.question: The domain controller holding the PDC Emulator role for contoso.local suffers unrecoverable hardware failure with no viable backup. No other role-transfer window is available before this affects users. What should the administrator do to restore that role's function?
options: Wait for the role to automatically fail over to another DC
Rebuild the failed DC with the same name and it will reclaim the role automatically
Seize the PDC Emulator role onto a surviving, healthy domain controller
Promote a new DC and manually copy the SYSVOL folder from a backup
questions.explanation: FSMO roles never fail over automatically — when the role holder is permanently gone, an administrator must seize the role onto a surviving DC (typically with PowerShell's Move-ADDirectoryServerOperationMasterRole -Force, or ntdsutil). Simply rebuilding a DC with the same name doesn't restore a role that was never transferred off cleanly.

questions.question: An organization has two Active Directory sites connected by a slow WAN link. Administrators notice changes made at one site take up to 15 minutes to appear at the other, while changes within the same site appear almost immediately. What explains this difference?
options: Inter-site replication runs on a configurable schedule and is compressed to conserve WAN bandwidth, while intra-site replication is near-immediate and uncompressed
The two sites are in different forests, so replication uses SMTP instead of RPC
Global Catalog servers replicate slower than non-GC domain controllers by design
FSMO role holders replicate on a separate, faster schedule than regular objects, independent of site topology
questions.explanation: This is exactly how intra-site vs. inter-site replication is designed to behave: intra-site uses change notification for near-real-time convergence, while inter-site replication is scheduled and compressed specifically to be considerate of limited WAN links. It has nothing to do with GC status, forest boundaries, or FSMO roles.

questions.question: Two companies with separate Active Directory forests merge and need users in either forest to authenticate to resources in the other, with the relationship extending automatically to every domain in both forests. Which trust should be configured?
options: A one-way external trust between the two root domains
A shortcut trust between the two forest roots
A realm trust to a non-Windows Kerberos environment
A two-way forest trust between the two forest root domains
questions.explanation: A forest trust is transitive across every domain within both forests, which is exactly what's needed here, and making it two-way lets authentication flow in either direction. An external trust is explicitly non-transitive and would need to be repeated between every domain pair, and a shortcut trust only optimizes referral paths within a single existing forest.
questions.whyTested: This tests whether you can match a specific transitivity and scope requirement to the right trust type instead of pattern-matching on the word 'trust' — AZ-802 stacks four trust types that all connect two AD environments in superficially similar ways, and the exam wants you to notice which one actually satisfies 'every domain in both forests' rather than a narrower relationship.

questions.question: A GPO linked at the domain level sets a screen lock timeout of 15 minutes. A GPO linked to a specific OU sets it to 5 minutes for higher-security accounts, and neither GPO is marked Enforced. Users in that OU report a 5-minute lockout. Why?
options: Domain-linked GPOs stop being evaluated once a GPO is also linked at the OU level
GPOs are processed in Local, Site, Domain, OU order, so the OU-linked GPO applies last and wins the conflict
The OU GPO must have Block Inheritance enabled to take precedence
Group Policy conflicts are resolved alphabetically by GPO name
questions.explanation: With neither GPO enforced, normal processing order (Local, Site, Domain, OU) applies, and the setting from whichever GPO is processed last — the one closest to the object, here the OU-linked GPO — wins. Block Inheritance affects whether higher-level GPOs apply at all, not which of two applying GPOs wins a setting conflict.
questions.whyTested: GPO precedence questions like this exist to check whether you've actually memorized the LSDOU processing order rather than reflexively reaching for Enforced or Block Inheritance whenever a GPO conflict shows up — this scenario deliberately has neither configured, so the exam is testing whether you know plain last-applied-wins is the default behavior before those override mechanisms even enter the picture.

questions.question: A company wants Microsoft Entra ID sign-in to keep working for users even during a brief on-premises Active Directory outage, without standing up and maintaining AD FS servers. Which Microsoft Entra Connect authentication method should they choose?
options: Password Hash Synchronization
Federation with AD FS
Pass-through Authentication
Seamless SSO used on its own with no other method
questions.explanation: Password Hash Synchronization stores a hash of the password hash in Microsoft Entra ID, so authentication can complete in the cloud even if on-premises AD is temporarily unreachable. Pass-through Authentication and Federation both validate the password against on-premises infrastructure at sign-in time, which fails if that infrastructure is down.

questions.question: A branch office with minimal physical security needs a local domain controller for fast logon, but the security team is worried about credential exposure if the hardware is stolen. Which deployment addresses this concern while still providing local authentication?
options: A Read-Only Domain Controller with a restrictive Password Replication Policy
A writable DC with BitLocker enabled and no other changes
A Global Catalog server with the Infrastructure Master role
A domain controller placed in its own dedicated forest
questions.explanation: An RODC caches credentials only for accounts explicitly permitted by its Password Replication Policy, and holds a filtered attribute set, so theft of the hardware exposes far fewer credentials than a writable DC would. BitLocker helps with data-at-rest but doesn't limit which credentials the DC caches in the first place.

questions.question: A company runs an application pool identity across four load-balanced IIS servers and wants a single service identity used for Kerberos authentication, with AD automatically rotating its password across all four servers with zero manual synchronization. What should they configure?
options: A single standalone Managed Service Account shared across all four servers
A group Managed Service Account (gMSA) authorized for use on all four servers
A shared domain user account with a manually scripted password rotation task
Four separate standalone MSAs, one per server, joined into a single security group
questions.explanation: A gMSA is specifically designed to be used across multiple hosts, with AD managing and replicating its password automatically to every server authorized to use it. A standalone MSA is explicitly tied to a single computer and cannot be shared this way — attempting it doesn't work regardless of grouping.

questions.question: A company wants to apply Azure Policy and centralized Azure Monitor alerting to a set of on-premises Windows Servers, without migrating any workloads into Azure. Which approach achieves this?
options: Enable Azure Arc-enabled servers with the Connected Machine agent on each server
Move each server into an Azure availability set
Install Windows Admin Center and connect it to the Azure portal
Configure ExpressRoute between the on-premises network and Azure
questions.explanation: Azure Arc-enabled servers projects an on-premises server into Azure Resource Manager via the Connected Machine agent, making Azure Policy, Monitor, and other Azure management services available to it without moving the workload at all. ExpressRoute only provides network connectivity, and Windows Admin Center is a separate on-premises management tool, not an Azure resource-projection mechanism.

questions.question: An organization manages a mix of Server Core and Desktop Experience servers across two sites and wants a single, modern, browser-based tool that can manage both without RDP, including servers with no local GUI at all. What should they deploy?
options: Remote Desktop Services with a full desktop session to each server
Windows Admin Center
Server Manager installed locally on every Server Core machine
A dedicated jump box running the full Desktop Experience for every managed server
questions.explanation: Windows Admin Center is exactly this: a browser-based management surface that works equally well against Server Core (which lacks a local GUI shell) and Desktop Experience servers, all from one gateway. Server Manager's full GUI can't run locally on Server Core at all, and RDP-based approaches add overhead this scenario doesn't need.

questions.question: An administrator wants to patch every node in a six-node Hyper-V failover cluster with the latest cumulative update, one node at a time, automatically draining each node's VMs to other nodes before it reboots. Which feature accomplishes this without manual live migration of each workload?
options: Cluster-Aware Updating (CAU)
Storage Replica
Network ATC
Scale-Out File Server
questions.explanation: CAU is built exactly for this: it orchestrates draining, patching, and rebooting each cluster node in turn with no manual live migration required. The other three options address storage replication, network configuration, and file-serving roles respectively, none of which handle patch orchestration.

questions.question: A company runs two standalone Hyper-V hosts, one at its primary site and one at a secondary site, with no Failover Clustering configured between them and no shared storage. They want a specific VM's changes replicated to the secondary host roughly every 30 seconds, with the ability to fail over manually if the primary host fails. Which feature fits without requiring a cluster?
options: Hyper-V Replica
Storage Spaces Direct
Cluster-Aware Updating
Scale-Out File Server
questions.explanation: Hyper-V Replica works between two standalone Hyper-V hosts with no clustering or shared storage required, replicating a VM asynchronously as often as every 30 seconds. The other three options all depend on Failover Clustering, which this scenario explicitly does not have.

questions.question: An organization is decommissioning an aging file server and wants to move its shares to a new server while preserving the old server's name and IP address, so client UNC paths keep working with no reconfiguration. Which tool is purpose-built for this?
options: Windows Server Migration Tools (WSMT)
Active Directory Migration Tool (ADMT)
Storage Migration Service
Printer Migration Wizard
questions.explanation: Storage Migration Service migrates files, shares, and their settings, and can then transfer the source server's name and IP address to the destination so clients see no change at all. WSMT and ADMT handle general role settings and AD objects respectively, not this identity-transfer step, and the Printer Migration Wizard is specific to print servers.

questions.question: A Hyper-V host has one physical NIC. Several VMs on that host need to reach resources on the physical LAN, and the host itself should also retain LAN connectivity through that same NIC. Which virtual switch type should be created?
options: A private virtual switch, which isolates VM-to-VM traffic on the host with no path out to the physical LAN
An internal virtual switch, which lets VMs and the host talk to each other but never reaches the physical NIC at all
External virtual switch with 'Allow management operating system to share this network adapter' enabled
No virtual switch at all, relying on a NAT network created directly through Windows' built-in ICS/NAT feature instead
questions.explanation: An external switch bound to the physical NIC gives VMs access to the physical network, and explicitly allowing the management OS to share that adapter keeps the host itself connected through the same NIC. A private switch isolates VMs from everything outside the host, and an internal switch alone doesn't reach the physical LAN at all.

questions.question: A new VM must support Secure Boot and UEFI firmware for compliance reasons. What must be true about how the VM is created?
options: It must be created as a Generation 1 VM with Secure Boot manually enabled afterward
Generation doesn't matter, as long as Secure Boot is enabled in the VM settings
It must be created as a Generation 2 VM, since only Generation 2 supports UEFI firmware and Secure Boot
It must run inside a Hyper-V isolated container instead of as a VM
questions.explanation: Secure Boot and UEFI firmware are only available on Generation 2 VMs — Generation 1 emulates legacy BIOS and has no UEFI support at all, and this can't be changed after the fact since a VM's generation is fixed at creation.

questions.question: An administrator wants to move a running, business-critical VM from one Hyper-V host to another with zero perceptible downtime for connected users, ahead of planned host maintenance. Which feature accomplishes this?
options: Hyper-V Replica, failing over to the already-replicated but offline copy at the secondary site
Exporting the VM's configuration and re-importing it on the new host, then powering it back on there
Taking a production checkpoint and manually applying it to a new VM created on the new host
Live Migration, given shared/SMB storage and compatible processors between hosts
questions.explanation: Live Migration is designed specifically to move a running VM between hosts with no perceptible downtime, provided the hosts share (or can access) the same storage and have compatible processors or Processor Compatibility Mode enabled. Hyper-V Replica failover is a DR action against an already-replicated but offline copy, not a live, zero-downtime move.
questions.whyTested: Live Migration, Hyper-V Replica, export/re-import, and checkpoints all involve moving or copying a VM in some sense, which is exactly why AZ-802 tests whether you know which one is actually a live, zero-downtime operation versus a DR failover or an offline, manual process — the wrong-sounding-right answers here are the ones that technically move a VM but violate the zero-perceptible-downtime requirement stated in the question.

questions.question: Two competing customers' workloads must run as containers on the same shared host, with a requirement that a kernel-level compromise in one customer's container cannot affect the other's. Which container isolation mode meets this requirement?
options: Process isolation, since it is the default mode
Hyper-V isolation, since each container runs its own kernel inside a lightweight utility VM
Either mode, since both provide equivalent kernel isolation
Nested virtualization without containers at all
questions.explanation: Hyper-V isolation gives each container its own kernel instance inside a lightweight utility VM, providing VM-grade separation appropriate for mutually distrusting tenants. Process isolation shares the host's single kernel across all containers, which does not meet a requirement for containing a kernel-level compromise.

questions.question: A company wants DNS records for a zone to replicate automatically and securely to every domain controller, with support for secure dynamic updates restricted to authenticated computers. Which zone type should they choose?
options: A standard secondary zone
An Active Directory-integrated zone
A stub zone
A standard primary zone stored only in a text file
questions.explanation: AD-integrated zones store zone data in Active Directory itself, giving automatic multi-master replication to every DC and enabling secure dynamic updates restricted to authenticated, authorized computers. A standard primary zone lacks that AD-based security and multi-master replication, and secondary/stub zones are read-only or partial by design.

questions.question: A branch office needs its own local DHCP server for resilience if the WAN link fails, but under normal conditions the central datacenter's DHCP server should handle all lease requests so IP assignment stays centrally managed. Which DHCP failover mode fits?
options: Load balance mode with a 50/50 split
No failover — configure two entirely separate, non-overlapping scopes
Hot standby mode, with the datacenter server as active and the branch server as standby
Load balance mode with the branch office server weighted higher
questions.explanation: Hot standby mode designates one server (the datacenter server, here) as active under normal conditions, with the other only stepping in if the active server becomes unreachable — exactly matching this requirement. Load balance mode has both servers actively answering requests all the time, which doesn't match wanting the datacenter server to normally handle everything.

questions.question: A company needs the most predictable latency and highest available bandwidth for a latency-sensitive hybrid application connecting an on-premises datacenter to Azure, and cost is a secondary concern compared to reliability. Which connectivity option best fits?
options: A single site-to-site VPN tunnel over the public internet
Point-to-site VPN configured on each application server
Public internet connectivity with no VPN, using only TLS for the application traffic
ExpressRoute, using a private, dedicated circuit from a connectivity provider
questions.explanation: ExpressRoute provides a private, dedicated circuit that avoids the public internet entirely, giving more predictable latency and higher available bandwidth than a VPN — matching a scenario where reliability outweighs cost. A site-to-site or point-to-site VPN both still ride over the variable public internet.

questions.question: A company deploys 802.1X authentication for wired switch ports and wants a centralized RADIUS server that can also handle VPN authentication requests from the same policy engine. What role should be deployed?
options: DFS Replication
Active Directory Certificate Services with no NPS role
Network Policy Server (NPS)
DHCP failover
questions.explanation: NPS is Microsoft's RADIUS server and proxy, capable of centralizing authentication and policy decisions for both 802.1X network access and VPN connections from one console. AD CS can issue the certificates 802.1X might use, but it isn't itself a RADIUS server, and DFS Replication/DHCP failover are unrelated to authentication.

questions.question: Users across three file servers need to access their files through a single, unified path like \\contoso\shares regardless of which physical server actually holds their folder. What should be deployed?
options: Data Deduplication on all three servers
Storage Replica between the three servers
DFS Namespaces, presenting one logical path across the three servers' shares
A single Storage Spaces Direct cluster replacing the three servers
questions.explanation: DFS Namespaces is exactly for this: presenting one logical folder structure that transparently maps to shares that may physically live on different servers. Data Deduplication and Storage Replica address disk-space efficiency and replication respectively, not a unified namespace.

questions.question: A company wants the actual contents of a critical shared folder kept synchronized in near real time across two file servers in different offices, so either server can serve current files if the other goes down. What should be configured?
options: DFS Namespaces only, with no replication configured
A stub zone linking the two servers
DFS Replication between the two servers' shared folders
Data Deduplication scheduled nightly on each server
questions.explanation: DFS Replication is the feature that actually synchronizes folder contents between multiple servers, which is what's needed for either server to serve current data. DFS Namespaces alone only provides a unified path — without replication behind it, the two servers' content could diverge with nothing keeping them in sync.

questions.question: A company is building a hyperconverged Hyper-V cluster using only local NVMe and SATA disks in each cluster node, with no separate SAN or shared storage array. Which technology pools that local storage into a single, cluster-wide software-defined storage pool?
options: DFS Namespaces
Data Deduplication
Azure File Sync
Storage Spaces Direct (S2D)
questions.explanation: Storage Spaces Direct pools local, direct-attached disks across the nodes of a failover cluster into shared software-defined storage, which is the definition of a hyperconverged deployment with no separate SAN. DFS Namespaces and Azure File Sync solve file-sharing and cloud-sync problems, not local disk pooling.

questions.question: A file server hosting mostly static reference documents and old project archives is running low on disk space. Nightly backups already run to a separate location. Which built-in feature would most directly reclaim space with minimal risk to a live, transactional workload?
options: Converting the volume to ReFS and using it as the new boot volume
Enabling Data Deduplication on the volume hosting those files
Enabling Storage Replica in synchronous mode
Moving the volume into a Storage Spaces Direct cluster
questions.explanation: Data Deduplication is well suited to exactly this kind of data — largely static files with a lot of duplicate content — and reclaims space with low risk since these aren't heavily, randomly modified transactional files. ReFS as a boot volume isn't supported at all, and Storage Replica and S2D solve replication and pooling problems, not space reclamation on an existing volume.

questions.question: A branch office file server is running out of local disk space, but users still expect to see and open their full folder structure, including files they rarely touch. The company wants those rarely used files' actual content to live in Azure while remaining transparently accessible. What should be deployed?
options: A larger local RAID 0 array with no cloud component
DFS Replication to an Azure VM running File Server
Storage Spaces Direct stretched to an Azure region
Azure File Sync with cloud tiering enabled
questions.explanation: Azure File Sync with cloud tiering keeps the full namespace visible locally while evicting cold files' actual content to Azure, retrieving it transparently on access — exactly the described need. The other options either add no cloud capacity at all or aren't designed for this kind of transparent, on-demand file tiering.

questions.question: A security team wants to prevent unauthorized executables from running on a fleet of Windows Server 2022 file servers, with policy enforcement happening at the kernel level before any unapproved binary can even start, surviving even if a local administrator account is compromised. Which technology should they deploy?
options: AppLocker
Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security
Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC)
Just Enough Administration (JEA)
questions.explanation: WDAC enforces code integrity at the kernel level system-wide, which is exactly what resists a compromised local administrator trying to run unapproved code. AppLocker enforces rules in user mode and is easier to bypass with sufficient local privilege, and JEA restricts what an admin can do in a PowerShell session but does not block arbitrary executables from running at all.
questions.whyTested: This question stacks two allowlisting technologies that solve the same general problem at different enforcement levels, plus two unrelated security tools, specifically to test whether you know WDAC's kernel-level enforcement is what survives a compromised local administrator — a detail that's easy to blur if you've only learned 'WDAC and AppLocker both do application control' without the level each one enforces at.

questions.question: An organization wants to stop an attacker who gains local administrator rights on a domain-joined server from extracting cached NTLM and Kerberos credentials from memory using a tool such as Mimikatz. Which feature specifically defends against this?
options: Credential Guard
BitLocker
Cluster-Aware Updating
Storage Replica
questions.explanation: Credential Guard isolates LSASS secrets inside a virtualization-based security container that even a local administrator cannot read directly, which is precisely the scenario described. BitLocker protects data at rest on disk and has no effect on credentials held in memory, and the other two options are unrelated high-availability and DR features.

questions.question: A helpdesk technician needs to look up the current local administrator password for a specific Windows Server so they can log on and troubleshoot it, without ever setting or knowing that password themselves ahead of time. Which feature both rotates and stores that password for retrieval?
options: Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA)
Windows LAPS
Protected Users group
Authentication policy silos
questions.explanation: Windows LAPS automatically rotates each server's local administrator password and stores it, in AD DS or Microsoft Entra ID, for retrieval by delegated staff — exactly the lookup-on-demand workflow described. gMSA manages a service account's password rather than a local administrator account, and the other two options control authentication restrictions, not password storage.

questions.question: A regulated company wants Windows Server security event logs, along with signals from Microsoft Defender for Identity, correlated together with alerts from its cloud workloads in a single security operations view, with automated response playbooks available. Which service should ingest this data?
options: Azure Update Manager
Windows Admin Center
Azure Site Recovery
Microsoft Sentinel
questions.explanation: Microsoft Sentinel is the cloud-native SIEM and SOAR platform built specifically to ingest and correlate signals like this across identity, servers, and cloud workloads, with automated playbooks for response. The other three tools serve entirely different purposes — patch management, server administration, and DR orchestration — with no SIEM or SOAR correlation capability.

questions.question: An administrator wants to capture a consistent, repeatable set of CPU, memory, and disk counters on a schedule, so the same metrics can be reviewed over time rather than being configured manually every time an issue comes up. Which Performance Monitor feature should they configure?
options: A metric alert rule
A Data Collection Rule
Reliability Monitor
A Data Collector Set
questions.explanation: A Data Collector Set groups counters, traces, and configuration into a single, reusable, schedulable job within Performance Monitor. A Data Collection Rule is the Azure Monitor Agent equivalent for cloud-side collection, Reliability Monitor tracks a stability index rather than arbitrary counters, and a metric alert only fires on a threshold rather than capturing ongoing data.

questions.question: A hybrid fleet includes both native Azure VMs and on-premises servers. The team wants one unified agent, with one shared configuration object defining exactly which logs and performance counters to collect and where to send them, deployed consistently across the whole fleet.
options: Windows Admin Center extensions only
Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) with a Data Collection Rule (DCR)
The legacy Log Analytics (MMA) agent
Windows Server Backup with a custom policy
questions.explanation: AMA is the unified, current agent for both Azure VMs and Arc-enabled on-premises servers, and a DCR is exactly the shared configuration object that defines what is collected and where it goes. The legacy MMA agent is what AMA replaces, and the other two options are unrelated to log and metric collection configuration.

questions.question: An operations team wants to write a query against collected log data using a chain of operators like where, summarize, and project to filter and shape results, then turn that same query directly into an automated alert. Which technology are they using?
options: PowerShell Desired State Configuration, declaring the desired state of a server and letting the engine enforce it
