Windows Server Migration Tools, scripting the transfer of roles and data to a new server
Kusto Query Language (KQL) against a Log Analytics workspace
Cluster-Aware Updating, orchestrating patch installation one cluster node at a time
questions.explanation: KQL's operator-chaining query style against a Log Analytics workspace is exactly what is described, and workspace-based queries can be promoted directly into log alert rules with minimal extra work. The other three options are unrelated configuration, migration, and patching tools respectively, with no query language of this kind.

questions.question: A hybrid organization wants to see patch compliance and schedule update installation for both its Azure VMs and its Arc-enabled on-premises servers from a single place in the Azure portal, rather than maintaining a separate on-premises patching tool for those on-premises machines.
options: Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) alone
Azure Update Manager
Storage Migration Service
A Data Collector Set
questions.explanation: Azure Update Manager centrally assesses and schedules updates across both native Azure VMs and Arc-enabled on-premises servers from the Azure portal. WSUS alone has no visibility into Azure-native VM patch state, and the other two options are unrelated to patch management entirely.

questions.question: After a server begins experiencing intermittent crashes, an administrator first wants a quick visual timeline correlating the crashes with recent installs or updates, before digging into the full, detailed event logs to confirm the exact cause. Which tool should they check first?
options: Azure Update Manager compliance dashboard
A Data Collection Rule audit log
Reliability Monitor
Storage Replica health report
questions.explanation: Reliability Monitor plots a rolling stability index and correlates dips with specific events like installs or updates, making it a good first stop for spotting when a problem started before diving into Event Viewer's more detailed logs. The other three options address patch compliance, log collection configuration, and storage replication health, not this kind of stability timeline.

questions.question: An RODC caches credentials only for the accounts explicitly permitted by its Password Replication Policy, rather than the whole domain's credentials.
questions.explanation: That is the entire security purpose of the Password Replication Policy — it limits which accounts' credentials an RODC is allowed to cache, so a compromised RODC exposes only a limited subset of credentials.

questions.question: A GPO marked as Enforced can still be overridden by enabling Block Inheritance on the target organizational unit.
questions.explanation: Enforcement specifically overrides Block Inheritance — an Enforced GPO's settings still apply to a child OU even if that OU has Block Inheritance turned on. Enforcement is designed to win exactly this kind of conflict.

questions.question: Microsoft Entra Connect's Password Hash Synchronization feature transmits users' recoverable plaintext passwords to Microsoft Entra ID.
questions.explanation: PHS synchronizes a hash of the on-premises password hash, never a plaintext or otherwise reversible password, to Microsoft Entra ID. This is a frequently tested distinction, since the name alone can make it sound less secure than it actually is.

questions.question: A Server Core installation can still be managed remotely with Windows Admin Center or PowerShell, even though it has no local desktop shell to log into.
questions.explanation: Server Core removes the local GUI shell and most graphical tools, but remote management via Windows Admin Center, PowerShell remoting, or RSAT from another machine works normally, which is exactly how Server Core is meant to be administered day to day.

questions.question: Azure Site Recovery for on-premises Hyper-V hosts uses the same Configuration Server and Process Server components that VMware-to-Azure replication relies on.
questions.explanation: Hyper-V-to-Azure replication uses the Hyper-V Replica provider built into the Hyper-V host itself. The Configuration Server, Process Server, and Master Target Server roles are specifically part of the VMware and physical-server replication architecture, not the Hyper-V one.

questions.question: Generation 2 Hyper-V virtual machines support UEFI firmware and Secure Boot, while Generation 1 machines emulate legacy BIOS.
questions.explanation: This is the core distinction between the two generations, and it's fixed at VM creation time — a Generation 1 VM cannot gain UEFI/Secure Boot support later without being recreated as Generation 2.

questions.question: Containers running under Hyper-V isolation each get their own lightweight utility VM and kernel instance, rather than sharing the host kernel the way process-isolated containers do.
questions.explanation: That extra utility-VM layer is exactly what gives Hyper-V isolation its stronger, VM-grade separation compared to process isolation, which shares a single host kernel across all its containers.

questions.question: DHCP failover in hot standby mode designates one server as active and the other as a passive backup, rather than splitting client load evenly between the two.
questions.explanation: That's the defining trait of hot standby mode, as opposed to load balance mode, where both servers actively answer requests according to a configured percentage split.

questions.question: A DNS stub zone stores a full, authoritative copy of every record in the delegated zone, the same way a secondary zone does.
questions.explanation: A stub zone stores only NS, SOA, and glue A/AAAA records — enough to know which servers are authoritative — not the zone's full record set. A secondary zone, by contrast, does hold a full read-only copy via zone transfer.

questions.question: Storage Replica can perform synchronous, block-level replication between two servers with zero data loss, provided latency between them is low enough.
questions.explanation: Synchronous replication in Storage Replica commits a write on both the source and destination before acknowledging it, guaranteeing zero data loss on failover — but it depends on latency being low enough that this round trip doesn't become a bottleneck, which is why it's typically used between nearby sites.

questions.question: ReFS (Resilient File System) is fully supported as a boot volume for the Windows Server operating system, just like NTFS.
questions.explanation: ReFS is not supported for the boot/system volume — Windows Server still requires NTFS there. ReFS is intended for data volumes, particularly ones backed by Storage Spaces where its self-healing and integrity-checking features can be fully used.

questions.question: Windows LAPS can store a managed local administrator password in Microsoft Entra ID for an Entra-joined device, not only in Active Directory Domain Services.
questions.explanation: Windows LAPS supports backing up the managed password to either Active Directory or Microsoft Entra ID depending on how the device is joined, which is part of what makes it usable across hybrid and cloud-joined fleets, not just traditional on-premises domain members.

questions.question: An account in the Protected Users group can still fall back to NTLM authentication if Kerberos is briefly unavailable.
questions.explanation: Protected Users membership removes the NTLM fallback entirely — if Kerberos cannot be used, authentication simply fails rather than falling back to a weaker protocol, which is the deliberate point of the control.

questions.question: A server must be Azure Arc-enabled, or be a native Azure VM, before Azure Update Manager can assess or patch it.
questions.explanation: Update Manager has no visibility into a plain on-premises server with no Arc agent and no Azure connection — Arc-enabling the server, or it being a native Azure VM, is the prerequisite that makes it visible to Update Manager at all.

questions.question: A single Data Collection Rule (DCR) in Azure Monitor can only be associated with one machine at a time, requiring a separate DCR to be authored for every server in a fleet.
questions.explanation: One DCR can be associated with many machines at once, which is what allows a single collection configuration to apply consistently across an entire hybrid fleet instead of being authored per server.

questions.question: Which two of the following FSMO roles exist once per domain rather than once per forest? (Choose two.)
options: RID Master
Schema Master
PDC Emulator
Domain Naming Master
questions.explanation: RID Master and PDC Emulator are domain-wide roles, existing once in every domain. Schema Master and Domain Naming Master are forest-wide roles, existing only once across the entire forest.

questions.question: Which two of the following are genuine Microsoft Entra Connect hybrid authentication methods? (Choose two.)
options: Kerberos Constrained Delegation
LDAP Simple Bind over an unencrypted connection
Password Hash Synchronization
Pass-through Authentication
questions.explanation: Password Hash Synchronization and Pass-through Authentication are both genuine Microsoft Entra Connect authentication methods (alongside Federation with AD FS). Kerberos Constrained Delegation and unencrypted LDAP simple bind are unrelated on-premises authentication/authorization mechanisms, not hybrid sign-in methods.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about Azure Arc-enabled servers? (Choose two.)
options: It requires migrating the server's actual workload into an Azure VM
It replaces the need for any on-premises Active Directory infrastructure
It installs a Connected Machine agent that projects the server into Azure Resource Manager
It lets you apply Azure Policy and Azure Monitor to an on-premises server without moving it
questions.explanation: Azure Arc's Connected Machine agent projects a server into Azure Resource Manager so Azure Policy, Monitor, and similar services can manage it, all without moving the workload itself. It has nothing to do with replacing on-premises AD, and it explicitly does not require migrating the workload into an Azure VM.

questions.question: Which two of the following correctly distinguish an in-place upgrade from a migration to a new server? (Choose two.)
options: An in-place upgrade keeps the same hardware or VM and updates the OS directly on it
A migration always requires reinstalling Active Directory Domain Services from scratch
A migration moves roles and data to a separate, already-provisioned destination server
An in-place upgrade is supported between any two Windows Server versions regardless of version gap
questions.explanation: An in-place upgrade updates the existing server directly, while a migration moves roles and data to a separate destination server, leaving the source untouched until cutover. Migrations do not require reinstalling AD DS from scratch, and in-place upgrades are explicitly not supported across every version gap — that is exactly when migration becomes necessary instead.

questions.question: A company is building a two-node failover cluster split across two small branch offices with no third site available to host a witness server. Which witness type best fits, and why?
options: Node Majority with no witness, since two nodes already form a majority together
Cloud Witness, since it only needs an Azure Storage account rather than a third physical site
Node and Disk Majority, using a shared disk located at one of the two branch offices
No witness is needed for any cluster with more than one node
questions.explanation: With only two nodes, a single node failure leaves just one vote — not a majority — so an extra witness vote is required to keep the cluster online; a plain Node Majority model cannot survive a node failure here. Cloud Witness supplies that extra vote from Azure Blob Storage, avoiding the need for a third physical site. A shared disk witness at one of the two branch offices would tie the witness's availability to that specific site's health, defeating the purpose of a tie-breaking vote.

questions.question: Skipping cluster validation (Test-Cluster) is fully supported by Microsoft as long as the cluster comes online successfully.
questions.explanation: A cluster that skips or fails validation is explicitly unsupported if a validation-related problem later causes an outage, even though Windows Server will still let such a cluster be created and come online.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about Hyper-V Live Migration? (Choose two.)
options: It always requires the VM to be shut down first
It requires the destination host to have a compatible processor or Processor Compatibility Mode enabled
It permanently deletes the VM's existing checkpoints before migrating
It can move a running VM between hosts with no perceptible downtime when properly configured
questions.explanation: Live Migration moves a running VM with no perceptible downtime, but it does require processor compatibility (or Processor Compatibility Mode) between the source and destination hosts. It neither requires shutting the VM down nor deletes existing checkpoints as part of the process.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about IP Address Management (IPAM)? (Choose two.)
options: IPAM must itself be configured to act as the domain's primary DHCP server
IPAM can centrally monitor and manage multiple DHCP and DNS servers from one console
IPAM helps track IP address utilization and detect overlapping or duplicate DHCP scopes
IPAM removes the need to ever configure a DHCP or DNS server role anywhere
questions.explanation: IPAM's job is centrally monitoring and managing existing DHCP and DNS servers, including tracking utilization and catching overlapping or duplicate scopes. It is not itself a DHCP server, and deploying it does not eliminate the need for separate DHCP/DNS server roles.

questions.question: Which two of the following correctly describe Storage Spaces resiliency types? (Choose two.)
options: Parity resiliency generally offers better write performance than mirroring
Simple resiliency spaces tolerate one disk failure without data loss
A two-way mirror can tolerate the loss of one physical disk without data loss
Parity resiliency is generally more storage-efficient than mirroring for the same fault tolerance
questions.explanation: A two-way mirror tolerates one disk failure, and parity is generally more storage-efficient than mirroring at similar fault tolerance — though at the cost of slower random writes, not better write performance. Simple resiliency has no redundancy at all and tolerates zero disk failures.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about DFS Namespaces? (Choose two.)
options: DFS Namespaces requires Data Deduplication to be enabled first
A domain-based namespace can have multiple namespace servers for redundancy
A standalone namespace's configuration is stored in Active Directory
A domain-based namespace stores its configuration in Active Directory
questions.explanation: A domain-based DFS namespace stores its configuration in Active Directory and can be hosted on multiple namespace servers for redundancy. A standalone namespace, by contrast, keeps its configuration in the local registry of a single server rather than in AD, and DFS Namespaces has no dependency on Data Deduplication.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about Microsoft Defender for Identity? (Choose two.)
options: It is installed as sensors directly on domain controllers
It replaces the need for a certification authority
It can detect on-premises attack techniques such as pass-the-hash and DCSync
It only monitors cloud sign-in activity, not on-premises AD DS
questions.explanation: Defender for Identity runs via sensors on domain controllers and is built specifically to detect on-premises identity attacks like pass-the-hash and DCSync. It has nothing to do with certificate issuance, and it is the opposite of cloud-sign-in-only — its whole focus is the on-premises identity plane.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about Azure Monitor alert rules? (Choose two.)
options: A metric alert evaluates a numeric signal against a threshold on a schedule
A log alert runs a KQL query on a schedule and fires based on its results
An action group defines the alert condition itself, not the response
Alert rules cannot be attached to Arc-enabled on-premises servers
questions.explanation: Metric alerts and log alerts are correctly described here — one evaluates a numeric threshold, the other runs a scheduled KQL query. An action group defines the response to a firing alert, not the condition, and Arc-enabled servers are exactly the kind of hybrid machine Azure Monitor alerting is designed to cover.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about Reliability Monitor and Event Viewer? (Choose two.)
options: Reliability Monitor plots a rolling stability index correlated with events like installs and crashes
Event Viewer provides detailed, filterable logs across System, Application, Security, and role-specific channels
Event Viewer and Reliability Monitor are two names for the exact same tool
Reliability Monitor replaces the need to ever open Event Viewer
questions.explanation: Reliability Monitor's stability-index timeline and Event Viewer's detailed, filterable logs are both accurately described, and they serve complementary rather than identical purposes — Reliability Monitor is typically a first look, and Event Viewer is where the detailed confirmation happens afterward, not a tool it replaces.

questions.question: An OU containing several user accounts, along with their group memberships, was deleted three days ago. The forest functional level is Windows Server 2016, and the AD Recycle Bin feature was enabled a year ago. What is the most complete way to recover the users with their original group memberships intact?
options: Perform a tombstone reanimation on each deleted user object, using ldp.exe against the object's tombstone lifetime window
Restore only from a full system state backup taken before the deletion, using Windows Server Backup's authoritative restore mode
Manually recreate each user account and re-add it to its original groups one at a time using Active Directory Users and Computers
Restore the deleted objects from the AD Recycle Bin, which preserves group memberships and most original attributes
questions.explanation: With the AD Recycle Bin already enabled, deleted objects can be restored with essentially all of their original attributes, including group memberships, directly from the Recycle Bin — the most complete and least disruptive option. Tombstone reanimation, the older method, recovers a bare object that has lost most of its link-valued attributes, including group memberships, which would then have to be manually re-added anyway. A full system-state restore risks rolling back unrelated changes made since the backup. Manually recreating accounts is slow and error-prone, and creates new SIDs that lose the objects' original permissions history.

questions.question: A Hyper-V Replica primary VM is about to undergo scheduled maintenance. The administrator wants to fail over to the replica VM at the secondary site with zero data loss, and wants the original primary to automatically become the new replica afterward. Which type of failover should be performed?
options: An unplanned failover, initiated immediately without checking the primary VM's status
A test failover, which brings the replica online in an isolated network only
A planned failover, initiated while the primary VM is still running and reachable
Failback using Hyper-V Live Migration instead of Replica failover
questions.explanation: A planned failover requires the primary VM to be shut down gracefully first, replicates any final changes so there is zero data loss, and automatically reverses replication direction so the original primary becomes the new replica — exactly matching a scheduled maintenance scenario. An unplanned failover is the emergency path used when the primary is already unreachable and may lose any changes since the last replication cycle. A test failover only verifies the replica in an isolated sandbox network without redirecting production traffic. Live Migration requires shared or replicated storage between hosts and isn't how Hyper-V Replica performs a site failover.

questions.question: Before applying a risky configuration change to a production domain controller running as a Hyper-V VM, an administrator wants to take a point-in-time snapshot that is safe to restore without corrupting the AD database, using Volume Shadow Copy Service inside the guest to ensure application consistency. Which checkpoint type should be used?
options: A production checkpoint, which uses VSS inside the guest for an application-consistent snapshot
A standard checkpoint, which captures memory and device state in a point-in-time snapshot without invoking VSS inside the guest
An automatic checkpoint, created automatically before a driver or configuration change to the VM's virtual hardware
A saved-state export, pausing the VM's execution and writing its memory to a saved-state file on disk
questions.explanation: A production checkpoint uses VSS inside the guest OS to create an application-consistent, restorable point-in-time copy, which is specifically safe to use against workloads like Active Directory or SQL Server. A standard checkpoint only captures memory and device state like a saved game and is not application-aware, making it unsafe to restore into a running domain controller. Automatic checkpoints are unrelated to this manual, deliberate risk-mitigation step, and a plain saved-state export isn't a checkpoint or restorable snapshot mechanism at all.

questions.question: A three-node Hyper-V failover cluster stores its VM virtual disks on a single shared LUN. The administrator wants every node to be able to simultaneously read and write to that LUN as a common namespace, so any node can quickly take ownership of a VM without dismounting and remounting the disk. What should be configured?
options: A dedicated disk resource owned exclusively by one node at a time
Cluster Shared Volumes (CSV), enabling simultaneous multi-node access to the same LUN
DFS Replication between each node's local disk
A Scale-Out File Server role with no cluster storage involved
questions.explanation: Cluster Shared Volumes let every node in the cluster simultaneously access the same LUN through a common namespace, which is exactly what allows a VM to move between nodes almost instantly without a slow, disruptive disk dismount/remount cycle. A traditional dedicated disk resource is owned by only one node at a time, forcing exactly that kind of handoff on failover. DFS Replication synchronizes file content between separate volumes, not simultaneous access to one shared LUN. A Scale-Out File Server is a separate SMB file-serving role that itself typically relies on CSV underneath it, not a substitute for it.

questions.question: A team wants Security and Application event log entries from 50 servers centralized onto a single collector server for review, without deploying Azure Monitor Agent or a Log Analytics workspace, using only built-in Windows Server functionality. Which feature should be configured?
options: Data Collector Sets, configured on the collector server and pointed at each of the 50 servers over WMI
Reliability Monitor, configured on the collector server to poll each of the 50 servers' stability index remotely
Windows Event Forwarding (WEF), using a subscription on the collector server and WinRM on each source server
Azure Update Manager, using its centralized reporting dashboard to pull patch and event data from each server
questions.explanation: Windows Event Forwarding uses WinRM-based subscriptions so a collector server can gather selected event log entries from many source servers into its own forwarded-events log, entirely with built-in Windows Server functionality and no Azure agent required. Data Collector Sets on the collector alone wouldn't gather anything from the other 50 servers, since they capture local performance and trace data. Reliability Monitor only tracks a single server's own stability index locally. Update Manager is a patch-compliance service, unrelated to centralizing event logs.

questions.question: An operations team manages a hybrid fleet of Azure VMs and Arc-enabled on-premises servers and wants a single view showing each server's running processes, discovered application dependencies, and connections to other servers, to help plan a migration and troubleshoot cross-server issues. Which Azure Monitor capability provides this?
options: Reliability Monitor
Windows Server Backup reporting
A Data Collector Set with only a CPU counter added
VM insights, using the dependency map feature
questions.explanation: VM insights' dependency map, built on the Dependency Agent alongside Azure Monitor Agent, specifically visualizes running processes and the discovered connections and dependencies between servers, which is exactly what's needed for migration planning and cross-server troubleshooting, across both Azure VMs and Arc-enabled on-premises servers. Reliability Monitor only tracks one server's local stability index, not cross-server dependencies. Windows Server Backup reporting covers backup job status, not process or dependency mapping. A Data Collector Set with just a CPU counter captures only that one local metric.

questions.question: In a multi-domain forest, a user who is a member of a universal group can fail to complete logon if no Global Catalog server is reachable at logon time.
questions.explanation: Universal group membership can only be resolved by querying a Global Catalog server, since only the GC holds a forest-wide partial replica listing universal group memberships; if none is reachable, logon can be blocked depending on caching settings. This is distinct from a single-domain forest, where a domain controller alone can fully resolve group membership without needing a GC at all.

questions.question: Just Enough Administration (JEA) lets an organization grant a support technician access to run a specific, limited set of PowerShell cmdlets under an elevated identity, without granting that technician full local administrator rights on the server.
questions.explanation: JEA constrains a PowerShell session to a defined set of cmdlets, parameters, and values via a role capability file, running the elevated operations under a virtual account behind the scenes, so the connecting user never actually receives full administrator rights on the machine. This is different from simply adding a user to the local Administrators group, which grants unrestricted access.

questions.question: Which two of the following correctly describe DNS record types used in a Windows Server environment? (Choose two.)
options: A PTR record maps an IP address back to a hostname, used for reverse lookups
An SRV record maps a hostname directly to an IP address, identical to an A record
A CNAME record is an alias that points to another hostname rather than directly to an IP address
An MX record is required for a domain controller to be discoverable by client computers
questions.explanation: A PTR record supports reverse lookup, resolving an IP address back to a hostname, and a CNAME record is an alias pointing to another hostname rather than directly to an IP address. An SRV record identifies the host and port for a specific service, such as locating domain controllers via _ldap._tcp SRV records — it is not the same as a simple A record mapping. MX records route mail delivery and have nothing to do with domain controller discovery, which instead relies on SRV records.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about the Volume Shadow Copy Service (VSS) and shadow copies of shared folders in Windows Server? (Choose two.)
options: Shadow copies replace the need for any regular backup solution entirely
Enabling shadow copies lets users restore an earlier version of a file themselves via the Previous Versions tab, without administrator intervention
Shadow copies are stored on a different physical server from the source volume by default
VSS shadow copies are taken on a schedule and only store the changed blocks since the previous shadow copy, not a full duplicate of the volume
questions.explanation: Shadow copies expose a self-service Previous Versions tab so users can recover an earlier file version without an administrator restoring from backup, and VSS is efficient because each shadow copy stores only the changed blocks since the previous one rather than a full volume duplicate. Shadow copies are a convenient point-in-time recovery aid, not a replacement for a real backup solution, and they live on the same volume/server by default rather than a different physical server, which is also why they don't protect against the loss of that server's hardware.

questions.question: Which feature lets an administrator restore a deleted user object, including its original group memberships, directly and quickly, without restoring from a backup?
options: The AD Recycle Bin
Tombstone reanimation alone
A full system state restore
The Protected Users group
questions.explanation: The AD Recycle Bin restores a deleted object with essentially all of its original attributes, including link-valued attributes like group memberships, with no backup restore needed. Tombstone reanimation, the older method, recovers a bare object that has already lost most linked attributes. A full system state restore works but is slower and riskier, since it can roll back unrelated changes, and the Protected Users group is an authentication hardening feature unrelated to object recovery.

questions.question: A single AD forest has two domains, sales.contoso.com and hr.contoso.com, both children of contoso.com. A user in sales.contoso.com needs to access a resource in hr.contoso.com. What lets this work without any administrator configuring a new trust?
options: The implicit, transitive parent-child trust that already exists between domains in the same forest
A manually created external trust between the two domains
A realm trust to a non-Windows Kerberos realm
A one-way shortcut trust configured by the administrator
questions.explanation: Parent-child trusts within a single forest are created automatically and are transitive, so no administrator action is needed for sales.contoso.com and hr.contoso.com to authenticate each other. External and realm trusts must always be explicitly created by an administrator, and a shortcut trust is an optional optimization added later to shorten an existing, already-working referral path — it isn't what enables access in the first place.

questions.question: A company Arc-enables 30 on-premises servers so they show up in the Azure portal, but Azure Update Manager still reports it has no update compliance data for them. What is most likely missing?
options: The Connected Machine agent is installed, but Update Manager still needs to be enabled for those specific machines before patch data starts reporting
Arc-enabled servers can never be patched through Update Manager — only native Azure VMs support it
The servers must first be migrated into Azure VMs before any patch data can appear
WSUS must be fully uninstalled from the network before Update Manager will report anything
questions.explanation: Arc projects a server into Azure Resource Manager, but update compliance reporting specifically requires Update Manager to be enabled for those machines on top of that — being Arc-enabled alone doesn't automatically start patch reporting. Update Manager fully supports Arc-enabled servers without any migration into a native Azure VM, and it has no dependency on removing WSUS from the network.

questions.question: Which Hyper-V VM generation is required if a virtual machine needs to boot from a virtual hard disk larger than 2 TB using GPT partitioning?
options: Generation 2
Generation 1
Either generation, since boot disk size has nothing to do with VM generation
Neither — a GPT boot disk isn't supported by Hyper-V at all
questions.explanation: Generation 2 VMs boot via UEFI and support a GPT boot volume larger than 2 TB. Generation 1 VMs emulate legacy BIOS and are limited to MBR boot disks capped at 2 TB, and this is fixed at creation time, not something that can be toggled afterward. GPT boot disks are fully supported in Hyper-V, just only on Generation 2.

questions.question: A company runs DHCP failover in load balance mode between two servers with an 80/20 split favoring the datacenter server. The branch server's WAN link then fails for several hours. What happens to DHCP service at the branch during the outage, and why?
options: Clients at the branch can still obtain and renew leases from the branch server alone, since load balance mode lets either partner keep answering independently from the shared scope's address pool
All DHCP service at the branch stops immediately, since load balance mode requires constant communication between partners to answer any request at all
The branch server automatically promotes itself into hot standby active mode until the link is restored
Clients at the branch fall back to APIPA addressing until the WAN link is restored, since no local DHCP server can operate independently
questions.explanation: In load balance mode, each partner can independently answer client requests from its own share of the address pool even when it can't currently reach its partner — it just can't synchronize new lease state with that partner until the link returns. It doesn't require constant partner communication to answer requests at all, it doesn't automatically convert into a different failover mode, and clients don't fall back to APIPA since the branch server keeps answering on its own.

questions.question: A team building a Storage Spaces Direct volume for a Hyper-V workload wants the volume to automatically detect and repair background bit-rot corruption without taking the volume offline. Which file system should they format the volume with to get this?
options: ReFS (Resilient File System)
NTFS, with periodic chkdsk runs scheduled as a background task
FAT32, since it has the simplest on-disk structure to scan
exFAT, since it's optimized for large removable media
questions.explanation: ReFS includes built-in integrity streams and background scrubbing that automatically detect and repair corruption online, especially when paired with Storage Spaces resiliency underneath it. NTFS relies on an offline chkdsk pass rather than automatic online repair, and FAT32/exFAT have no equivalent integrity-checking mechanism and aren't used for Hyper-V storage volumes at all.

questions.question: A finance team needs a specific SQL Server database's data files replicated block-for-block to a second site with guaranteed byte-for-byte consistency for a clustered failover, while a separate team just needs a shared folder of loosely edited spreadsheets kept roughly in sync across two offices for convenience. Which pairing of technologies fits each need respectively?
options: Storage Replica for the SQL Server data files; DFS Replication for the shared spreadsheet folder
DFS Replication for the SQL Server data files; Storage Replica for the shared spreadsheet folder
Storage Replica for both, since it is the newer technology and supersedes DFS Replication entirely
DFS Replication for both, since it works equally well at the block level and the file level
questions.explanation: Storage Replica performs block-level, application-agnostic replication with byte-for-byte consistency, suited to a clustered SQL Server data volume. DFS Replication is a file-level, multi-master sync feature built for loosely edited shared folders, not for the block-level consistency a SQL cluster needs. Swapping the two applies the wrong granularity to each workload. Storage Replica hasn't replaced DFS Replication — they solve different problems, and DFS Replication doesn't operate at the block level at all.

questions.question: A hardened server has both Windows LAPS and Credential Guard deployed. An attacker who gains local administrator rights on that server tries to (1) look up the local administrator's own password, and (2) extract other users' cached credentials from LSASS memory using a tool like Mimikatz. Which of these two actions does Credential Guard block?
options: Only the LSASS credential-extraction attempt (2); Credential Guard has no bearing on LAPS-managed password storage or retrieval
Both actions (1) and (2), since Credential Guard supersedes LAPS entirely
Only the LAPS password lookup (1); Credential Guard has no effect on LSASS credential extraction
Neither action, since Credential Guard only protects Kerberos tickets, not NTLM or other LSASS secrets
questions.explanation: Credential Guard isolates LSASS secrets, including cached NTLM and Kerberos credentials, inside a virtualization-based security container, blocking Mimikatz-style extraction — but it has nothing to do with where or how LAPS stores or exposes the local administrator password, which is retrieved through Entra ID or AD DS delegation instead. Credential Guard also protects more than just Kerberos tickets; it covers NTLM secrets held in LSASS too.

questions.question: A team wants to be paged within a minute if a server's disk queue length spikes, and separately wants a weekly report correlating that same spike with any application deployments that happened around the same time. Which combination of Azure Monitor capabilities fits each need respectively?
options: A metric alert on disk queue length for the near-immediate page; a scheduled KQL query joining performance and deployment log data in Log Analytics for the weekly correlation report
A log alert running a KQL query every minute for the page; a Data Collector Set for the weekly correlation report
Reliability Monitor for the near-immediate page; a metric alert for the weekly correlation report
A single Data Collection Rule for both needs, since one DCR can both page on-call staff and generate scheduled reports
questions.explanation: Metric alerts evaluate lightweight numeric thresholds fast enough for near-real-time paging, while a scheduled KQL query joining performance and deployment data is exactly the tool for a periodic, multi-source correlation report — matching each need to the mechanism built for its latency and complexity. A log alert every single minute is a heavier, slower mechanism than a metric alert for fast threshold paging, and a Data Collector Set only captures local counters, producing no correlation report on its own. Reliability Monitor and a metric alert are swapped into the wrong roles, and a DCR only defines what's collected and where it's sent — it doesn't page anyone or generate a report by itself.

questions.question: An administrator accidentally deletes an OU containing 200 user accounts, and the deletion has already replicated to every domain controller in the domain. A system state backup taken the night before still has the OU intact. Which restore approach correctly brings the OU back without those objects simply being deleted again by normal replication?
options: A non-authoritative restore of the affected domain controller from the backup
An authoritative restore of the OU, performed in Directory Services Restore Mode
A full forest recovery using the Install-ADDSForest cmdlet
Reinstalling AD DS on the domain controller and rejoining it to the domain
questions.explanation: An authoritative restore, performed from Directory Services Restore Mode with ntdsutil, specifically marks the restored OU as authoritative so it replicates out and overwrites the deletion on every other domain controller. A plain non-authoritative restore would just let the restored DC's replication partners catch it back up to the deleted state, undoing the restore. A full forest recovery and reinstalling AD DS are far more disruptive responses to a single deleted OU.

questions.question: Microsoft Entra Domain Services provisions a fully managed, domain-joinable AD DS domain in Azure, which is a different service from Microsoft Entra Connect's identity synchronization.
questions.explanation: Microsoft Entra Domain Services creates and manages an actual AD DS domain in Azure for domain-join scenarios, while Microsoft Entra Connect only synchronizes identity objects into Microsoft Entra ID for cloud sign-in — they address different problems and are commonly used side by side rather than being the same service.

questions.question: A hosting provider needs far more compute and storage capacity than a single failover cluster's node-count ceiling allows, but still wants VMs to live-migrate seamlessly across that larger pool. Which feature is built for this scale?
options: Cluster-Aware Updating, extended to patch more nodes per run
A cluster set, grouping multiple member clusters into one larger fabric
Storage Spaces Direct, scaled to its maximum single-cluster node count
Hyper-V Replica, replicating VMs between every cluster in the datacenter
questions.explanation: A cluster set groups several separate failover clusters into one larger software-defined fabric so VMs can live-migrate across member-cluster boundaries, scaling well beyond a single cluster's node limit. CAU only orchestrates patching and adds no capacity, S2D is still bounded by one cluster's own node-count ceiling, and Hyper-V Replica is a DR replication tool, not a capacity-pooling mechanism.

questions.question: Hyper-V Replica extended replication requires tearing down the existing primary-to-replica relationship before a third copy of the VM can be configured.
questions.explanation: Extended replication is layered on top of an already-working primary-to-replica pair, adding a third, asynchronously replicated copy at a second replica host — it doesn't require removing or reconfiguring the existing replication relationship first.

questions.question: A development team builds a container image on a newer Windows Server base image, then tries to run it process-isolated on an older Windows Server host. The container fails to start with a version-mismatch error. What is the most direct fix that keeps the container process-isolated?
options: Rebuild the container image against a matching base image build
Add more memory to the Hyper-V host running the container
Switch the Hyper-V virtual switch from internal to external mode
Enable Credential Guard on the container host
questions.explanation: Process-isolated containers share the host kernel directly, so the container's base image build has to match (or be compatible with) the host OS build — rebuilding against a matching base image is the direct fix. Memory, virtual switch type, and Credential Guard have nothing to do with kernel build compatibility between a container image and its host.

questions.question: A hosting provider's fabric administrators have full console and hypervisor access to every Hyper-V host, but tenants require that not even those administrators be able to inspect a tenant VM's memory or disk contents. Which feature is designed specifically for this threat model?
options: Credential Guard, isolating LSASS secrets from the fabric administrator
Shielded virtual machines, attested and key-released through the Host Guardian Service
Windows Defender Application Control, blocking unapproved code on the host
BitLocker alone, enabled on the host's own boot volume
questions.explanation: Shielded VMs encrypt a tenant VM's disk and state and restrict even a fabric administrator from inspecting or console-connecting to it, with the Host Guardian Service attesting the host is trusted before releasing the needed key — exactly the hosting-provider threat model described. Credential Guard protects LSASS secrets on a single machine, not a tenant VM's contents from its own host's administrator, WDAC controls what code runs rather than who can inspect a VM, and BitLocker on the host's own boot volume doesn't protect a guest VM's contents from that host's administrators at all.

questions.question: In NAT networking mode, a Windows container gets a private IP address behind address translation on the host, rather than appearing directly on the physical network.
questions.explanation: NAT mode is Docker's default on Windows and gives each container a private, host-translated IP — transparent mode is the one that connects a container directly to the physical network as its own host.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about Host Guardian Service (HGS) attestation for shielded VMs? (Choose two.)
options: TPM-trusted attestation relies on hardware-based measurements of the host
Admin-trusted attestation is the stronger of the two attestation modes
A host must be attested as healthy and trusted before HGS releases the key needed to run the shielded VM
HGS attestation replaces the need for BitLocker on the shielded VM's virtual disk
questions.explanation: TPM-trusted attestation uses hardware-based measurements of the host, and HGS only releases the key needed to run a shielded VM after that attestation confirms the host is healthy and trusted. Admin-trusted attestation is actually the weaker of the two modes, not the stronger one, and HGS attestation works alongside BitLocker encryption on the VM's disk rather than replacing it.

questions.question: An administrator needs a quick way to connect a single on-premises test server to resources in an Azure virtual network, without manually configuring RRAS, certificates, or a VPN gateway by hand. Which Windows Admin Center feature fits?
options: Azure Network Adapter, provisioning a point-to-site VPN connection automatically
Azure File Sync, syncing the server's file share into the virtual network
Cluster-Aware Updating, draining the server before connecting it
Storage Migration Service, migrating the server's shares into Azure
questions.explanation: Azure Network Adapter automatically provisions a point-to-site VPN connection from the server into an Azure virtual network with none of the manual RRAS, certificate, or gateway configuration otherwise required. The other three options sync files, orchestrate patching, or migrate shares — none of them establish network connectivity into a virtual network.

questions.question: Routing and Remote Access Service (RRAS) is the component that actually terminates VPN connections, while Network Policy Server (NPS) separately handles the RADIUS authentication decision for them.
questions.explanation: RRAS (or a third-party VPN device) terminates the VPN connection itself and forwards the authentication request to NPS, which makes the RADIUS authentication and policy decision — the two roles are commonly paired but serve distinct jobs.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about Azure Network Adapter? (Choose two.)
options: It establishes a point-to-site VPN connection from the server into an Azure virtual network
It is the recommended way to connect two entire on-premises networks together at production scale
It can be configured directly from Windows Admin Center without manually building the VPN by hand
It permanently migrates the on-premises server's workload into the target virtual network
questions.explanation: Azure Network Adapter sets up a point-to-site VPN from the server into an Azure virtual network, configurable straight from Windows Admin Center without hand-building RRAS, certificates, or a gateway. It isn't meant for connecting two entire networks at production scale — a Site-to-Site VPN or ExpressRoute fits that instead — and it only provides connectivity; it doesn't migrate the server's workload anywhere.

questions.question: A department shares a single folder, and management wants to both cap each user's storage at 5 GB and block anyone from saving .mp3 files there, without changing any NTFS permissions. Which Windows Server feature provides both controls?
options: Data Deduplication, configured with a per-user exclusion list
File Server Resource Manager, using a quota and a file screen
Storage Replica, configured in asynchronous mode
DFS Namespaces, with a per-user folder target
questions.explanation: FSRM provides exactly these two independent controls: a quota caps total space per user or folder, and a file screen blocks specific file types regardless of how much space remains — neither requires touching NTFS permissions. Data Deduplication reclaims duplicate space rather than enforcing limits, and Storage Replica and DFS Namespaces address replication and unified paths, not per-user quotas or file-type blocking.

questions.question: A Scale-Out File Server lets every node in the cluster serve the same SMB share simultaneously and actively, unlike a traditional clustered file server where only one node owns a share at a time.
questions.explanation: That active-active access across all nodes, built on Cluster Shared Volumes, is exactly what distinguishes a Scale-Out File Server from a traditional general-use clustered file server, where ownership of a given share moves between nodes one at a time on failover.

questions.question: A security team wants a help-desk technician to be able to restart a specific set of services and clear specific event logs on a file server, under an elevated identity, but must not grant that technician's own account general local administrator rights on the box. Which feature should be configured?
options: Add the technician's account to the local Administrators group, restricted by a logon script
Just Enough Administration (JEA), with a role capability file scoped to those cmdlets
Windows LAPS, so the technician can retrieve the local administrator password on demand
The Protected Users security group, applied to the technician's own account
questions.explanation: JEA constrains a PowerShell session to a specific, defined set of cmdlets and parameters via a role capability file, running them under a virtual account — exactly matching a narrowly scoped task without granting full administrator rights. Adding the account to local Administrators grants broad, unrestricted access regardless of any logon script, Windows LAPS only manages the local administrator password itself rather than scoping what commands someone can run, and Protected Users restricts how an account authenticates, not what it's authorized to do once signed in.

questions.question: An authentication policy silo can restrict a group of related high-privilege accounts so they can only authenticate to and from a defined set of devices, limiting how far a compromised low-value account could reach.
questions.explanation: That containment is exactly the point of an authentication policy silo — it groups accounts and the specific devices or servers they're allowed to touch into one boundary, so even a compromised account outside that boundary can't be used to reach into it.

questions.question: An administrator sets up Windows Event Forwarding so a collector server gathers specific events from 200 source servers spread across multiple sites, without having to individually configure each source server's subscription settings one at a time. Which WEF subscription type fits this scale?
options: A collector-initiated (pull) subscription, listing every source server by name
A source-initiated (push) subscription, applied to source servers via Group Policy
A Data Collection Rule, pushed from Azure Monitor to each source server
A Data Collector Set, scheduled identically on all 200 servers
questions.explanation: A source-initiated (push) subscription lets a GPO point many source servers at the collector at once, without the administrator individually naming and configuring each source server the way a collector-initiated (pull) subscription requires — which is exactly what scales to 200 machines across multiple sites. A Data Collection Rule and a Data Collector Set are Azure Monitor Agent and Performance Monitor concepts respectively, not part of Windows Event Forwarding's subscription model at all.

questions.question: VM insights' dependency map relies on a separate Dependency Agent installed alongside Azure Monitor Agent to discover process-level connections between servers.
questions.explanation: Azure Monitor Agent alone collects logs and performance counters, but the dependency map specifically needs the separate Dependency Agent to discover and visualize process-level connections and dependencies between servers — without it, VM insights still shows performance data but not the dependency map itself.

questions.question: A company needs its internal AD DS-authenticated users to single sign-on to a third-party SaaS application using claims-based federation, while keeping the AD FS servers themselves out of the perimeter network and never directly reachable from the internet. What should be deployed in front of the AD FS farm?
options: A Web Application Proxy (WAP) server in the perimeter network, relaying requests to the internal AD FS farm
A second AD FS farm placed directly in the perimeter network
A Read-Only Domain Controller placed in the perimeter network
Microsoft Entra Domain Services, exposed directly to the internet
questions.explanation: Web Application Proxy is the reverse-proxy role built specifically to publish an internal AD FS farm (or other web applications) to external clients, so the AD FS servers themselves never sit in, or are reachable directly from, the perimeter network. Placing a second AD FS farm in the perimeter network defeats the purpose of keeping AD FS internal, and neither an RODC nor Microsoft Entra Domain Services performs claims-based federation or proxies AD FS traffic.

questions.question: Group Policy Modeling in GPMC requires the target computer or user to be online and reachable, while Group Policy Results only simulates what would apply without contacting a live target.
questions.explanation: This is reversed — Group Policy Modeling is the what-if simulation that does not require the target to be online, while Group Policy Results queries an actual, already-online target to show what really applied, which is closer to what gpresult reports from the command line.

questions.question: An operations team onboards a batch of Azure Arc-enabled servers and wants them to automatically receive, and keep, a consistent set of Microsoft-recommended configurations — covering things like Defender for Cloud, Update Manager, and Change Tracking and Inventory — with drift corrected automatically if someone changes a setting locally, instead of configuring each service by hand on every server. What should they enable?
options: Cluster-Aware Updating on each server
Azure Automanage machine configuration
Storage Migration Service against each server
Windows Admin Center alone, with no Azure connection
questions.explanation: Azure Automanage machine configuration applies, and continuously re-applies if it drifts, a consistent best-practice configuration across onboarded Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers, which is exactly this scenario. Cluster-Aware Updating only orchestrates cluster patching, Storage Migration Service migrates file shares, and Windows Admin Center on its own has no mechanism to continuously enforce a best-practice configuration set across many servers.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about Azure Automanage machine configuration? (Choose two.)
options: It applies to both native Azure VMs and Azure Arc-enabled on-premises servers
It requires an administrator to manually reconfigure each best-practice setting after onboarding
It continuously re-applies its configured best practices if a setting drifts locally
It replaces the need for a server to be Azure Arc-enabled at all
questions.explanation: Automanage applies to both native Azure VMs and Arc-enabled on-premises servers, and its defining behavior is continuously re-applying its configured best practices when local drift is detected, rather than a one-time setup. It specifically removes the need to manually reconfigure each setting by hand, and a non-Azure server still needs to be Arc-enabled first — Automanage builds on that enrollment rather than replacing it.

questions.question: A trainer wants a single Hyper-V VM to itself run Hyper-V and host child VMs inside it, simulating an entire Hyper-V host for a classroom lab without provisioning separate physical hardware per student. Which capability makes this possible?
options: Nested virtualization, exposing virtualization extensions into the VM
Dynamic Memory, raising the VM's memory ceiling as needed
Live Migration, moving the VM between two physical hosts
Switch Embedded Teaming on the physical host's NICs
questions.explanation: Nested virtualization exposes virtualization extensions from the physical host down into a running VM, letting that VM itself run Hyper-V and host child VMs — exactly what a single-VM classroom lab simulating a whole host needs. Dynamic Memory only adjusts a VM's own memory allocation, Live Migration moves a VM between hosts rather than enabling virtualization inside one, and SET is a networking feature unrelated to running a hypervisor inside a VM.

questions.question: A VM runs a SQL Server instance whose buffer pool is carefully sized and tuned, and the database team reports that the workload performs unpredictably whenever the VM's available memory changes while it's running. What Hyper-V memory configuration should replace whatever is currently assigned?
options: Static memory, fixing the VM's allocation at one constant value
Dynamic Memory, with a higher configured maximum than before
Dynamic Memory, with a lower configured minimum than before
Smart Paging only, with no change to the memory type
questions.explanation: Static memory fixes a VM's allocation permanently, which is exactly what a workload that tunes its own memory internally, like a SQL Server buffer pool, needs — it doesn't tolerate its available memory being raised or lowered by the host while running. Adjusting Dynamic Memory's maximum or minimum still leaves the VM's memory able to change at runtime, which is the behavior causing the unpredictable performance in the first place.

questions.question: Running Update-VMVersion to upgrade a VM's configuration version to a newer host's latest supported version is reversible, allowing the VM to later move back to a host that only supports the older version.
questions.explanation: Upgrading a VM's configuration version with Update-VMVersion is a one-way step — once completed, the VM can no longer move to, or live-migrate to, a host that only supports the older configuration version.

questions.question: A Hyper-V host has multiple RDMA-capable NICs, and the team wants to team them directly inside a Hyper-V virtual switch for converged storage and tenant traffic, while keeping RDMA working on the teamed adapters. Which teaming technology should they use?
options: Switch Embedded Teaming (SET)
Classic NIC Teaming (LBFO)
A single untamed NIC with no teaming at all
Routing and Remote Access Service (RRAS) load balancing
questions.explanation: Switch Embedded Teaming combines NICs directly inside a Hyper-V virtual switch while keeping RDMA working on the teamed adapters, which classic NIC Teaming (LBFO) cannot do — LBFO is not compatible with RDMA-capable adapters at all. A single untamed NIC provides no redundancy, and RRAS has nothing to do with teaming physical network adapters.

questions.question: DNS Policies let a Windows Server DNS server return different responses to the identical query based on criteria such as the client's subnet or the time of day, without changing the zone's underlying primary records.
questions.explanation: DNS Policies evaluate criteria like client subnet, time of day, or server health and select among zone scopes to decide which stored answer to return, all without editing the zone's actual primary records — useful for directing clients to their closest datacenter or pulling a failed site out of rotation.

questions.question: A server connects to the same iSCSI storage target over two separate network adapters and cables for redundancy, and the team wants Windows to automatically fail over to the surviving path if one drops, while also balancing I/O across both paths when they're both healthy. Which feature should be configured?
options: Multipath I/O (MPIO)
NIC Teaming across the two adapters
DFS Namespaces pointing at both paths
Storage Replica in asynchronous mode
questions.explanation: MPIO is built specifically to manage multiple physical paths to the same storage target, failing over automatically and optionally load-balancing I/O across the healthy paths. NIC Teaming combines network adapters for general network traffic rather than managing redundant storage paths to one target, and DFS Namespaces and Storage Replica solve unified-path and replication problems, not path failover to a single iSCSI target.

questions.question: A company wants each employee's personal documents kept in sync across their laptop and desktop, sourced from a central on-premises file share, with the ability to selectively wipe those synced corporate files from a lost device — without redirecting the user's entire profile folder structure to the server. Which feature fits best?
options: Work Folders
DFS Replication between the two devices
A plain mapped network drive on each device
Storage Replica in synchronous mode
questions.explanation: Work Folders syncs a designated folder of a user's own files between their devices and a central on-premises share, and supports policies like selective wipe from a lost device, without the full scope of Folder Redirection. DFS Replication and Storage Replica synchronize server-side shared folders or volumes rather than one user's files out to their personal devices, and a plain mapped drive offers no offline sync or selective-wipe capability at all.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about thin provisioning in Storage Spaces? (Choose two.)
options: A thin-provisioned virtual disk only consumes pool capacity as data is actually written to it
A thin-provisioned virtual disk immediately reserves its full configured size from the pool
Several thin-provisioned virtual disks can have combined logical sizes larger than the pool's actual physical capacity
Thin provisioning removes any need to monitor pool capacity over time
questions.explanation: A thin-provisioned virtual disk draws from the pool only as data is actually written, which is what lets several thin disks' combined logical sizes exceed the pool's real physical capacity. A fixed-provisioned disk, not a thin one, reserves its full size immediately, and thin provisioning actually increases the need to monitor pool capacity over time, since an under-watched pool can run out of real space unexpectedly.

questions.question: A company deploying Active Directory Certificate Services wants its root CA kept powered down and offline except when issuing or revoking a subordinate CA's certificate, with a separate, online CA actually handling day-to-day certificate requests from users and computers. Which deployment model is this?
options: A single-tier hierarchy with one Enterprise root CA handling everything
A two-tier hierarchy with an offline root CA and an online issuing (subordinate) CA
A Standalone CA with no AD DS integration at all
A certificate authority hosted entirely by Microsoft Entra Domain Services
questions.explanation: A two-tier hierarchy — an offline root CA plus an online issuing (subordinate) CA — is exactly this pattern, and it limits the blast radius of a compromise, since the root CA's key is never exposed on a day-to-day, network-connected server. A single-tier hierarchy would require the root CA itself to stay online and issue certificates directly, and a Standalone CA lacks the AD DS integration needed for automatic enrollment via certificate templates and Group Policy that most organizations also want alongside this.

questions.question: A Standalone CA automatically integrates with AD DS to support certificate auto-enrollment via Group Policy, the same way an Enterprise CA does.
questions.explanation: A Standalone CA has no AD DS integration and requires an administrator to manually approve each certificate request — automatic enrollment via certificate templates and Group Policy is specifically an Enterprise CA capability.

questions.question: A security team wants to start hardening its domain's GPOs from Microsoft's own documented, recommended baseline settings for its specific Windows Server version, rather than building a security-focused GPO's settings from scratch, and wants a tool to compare its current GPOs against that baseline. What should they use?
options: The Security Compliance Toolkit, with its Policy Analyzer and baseline GPOs
Windows Defender Application Control in audit mode
The Protected Users security group
Best Practices Analyzer, run against the Hyper-V role
questions.explanation: The Security Compliance Toolkit packages Microsoft's recommended GPO security baselines for a given OS version, along with a Policy Analyzer tool to compare a live GPO against that baseline — exactly the documented starting point and comparison capability described. WDAC controls code execution rather than baseline GPO settings, Protected Users is an account-authentication control, and Best Practices Analyzer checks a role's own configuration rules, not GPO security baselines.

questions.question: Right after promoting a new domain controller, an administrator wants a quick, built-in check of its AD DS configuration against Microsoft's own best-practice rules for that role, without deploying any Azure agent or external monitoring tool. Which tool should they use?
options: Best Practices Analyzer (BPA) in Server Manager
Reliability Monitor
A Data Collector Set with no counters configured
VM insights and the dependency map
questions.explanation: Best Practices Analyzer is a built-in Server Manager tool that scans an installed role, such as AD DS, against Microsoft's own best-practice configuration rules, with no Azure agent or external tool required. Reliability Monitor tracks a stability index over time rather than checking role configuration, an empty Data Collector Set captures nothing useful, and VM insights' dependency map visualizes cross-server process dependencies, not a single role's configuration against best practices.

questions.question: Change Tracking and Inventory records software, file, and registry changes over time for both Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers, using the same Azure Monitor Agent and Data Collection Rules already used for other monitoring data.
questions.explanation: Change Tracking and Inventory is delivered through the same Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) and Data Collection Rule (DCR) infrastructure used for other monitoring data, and works across both native Azure VMs and Azure Arc-enabled on-premises servers.

lessons.title: Active Directory Domain Services
lessons.summary: FSMO roles and replication, trusts and functional levels, Group Policy precedence, and the recovery and hybrid-identity tools built around AD DS.
lessons.reading:
Active Directory relies on a handful of specialized domain controller roles and mechanisms rather than treating every DC as perfectly interchangeable. The five FSMO roles split into two scopes: forest-wide (one per forest) are the Schema Master and Domain Naming Master, while domain-wide (one per domain) are the RID Master, PDC Emulator, and Infrastructure Master. The PDC Emulator specifically handles time synchronization and urgent password-change processing across the domain, so its unrecoverable loss with no available backup calls for seizing the role onto a healthy DC rather than waiting for a transfer window that no longer exists. The Infrastructure Master fixes cross-domain group-membership references, and shouldn't sit on a Global Catalog server unless every DC in the domain is also a GC — a Global Catalog server holds a full, writable copy of its own domain plus a partial, read-only copy of every other domain in the forest, which is what makes forest-wide searches and universal group membership resolution possible during logon. Without a reachable GC, a user in a multi-domain forest signing in with a UPN, or one belonging to a universal group, can actually be blocked from completing logon, since only the GC can resolve universal group membership.

Replication behaves differently depending on whether it's happening within a site or between sites. Intra-site replication is frequent, triggered by change notification, and uncompressed, following a ring topology the Knowledge Consistency Checker (KCC) builds automatically. Inter-site replication instead runs on a configured schedule over site links, compressed to conserve WAN bandwidth — which is exactly why changes at one site can take up to fifteen minutes to show up at another, while changes within a single site appear almost immediately. A site link's cost and replication interval control how the KCC actually builds the inter-site spanning tree, with lower cost preferred, and bridgehead servers are the specific DCs that do the actual replicating across that link.

Trust relationships connect separate parts of Active Directory together, and telling their types and transitivity apart is a frequent exam focus. A forest trust is transitive across two entire forests — every domain in one forest can authenticate to every domain in the other — which is exactly what two merging companies with separate forests need if they want that relationship to extend automatically to every domain on both sides. An external trust is non-transitive, linking two specific domains only, often across forests. A shortcut trust shortens the referral path between two domains that sit deep in the same forest, and a realm trust connects a domain to a non-Windows Kerberos realm. It's worth remembering that transitive doesn't mean unlimited: a forest trust doesn't automatically extend to some third forest that one of the two trusted forests happens to also trust. Within a single forest, though, two domains that are both children of the same parent domain — like sales.contoso.com and hr.contoso.com under contoso.com — already have an implicit, automatic two-way transitive trust with each other, with no administrator needing to configure anything new. Sitting above all of this, domain and forest functional levels gate which AD DS features are actually available, based on the oldest domain controller operating system version the domain or forest still has to support — raising the functional level unlocks newer features, like the AD Recycle Bin, but it's a one-way decision, since an older-OS domain controller can never be added back afterward.

Group Policy objects apply in a defined order — Local, Site, Domain, OU (LSDOU) — and, in a plain conflict with nothing special configured, the last one applied, the OU closest to the actual object, normally wins. Enforced changes that default, overriding the normal order and always winning, even against Block Inheritance configured on a child OU — enforcement beats blocking, not the other way around, which is a very common exam trap. Group Policy settings are strictly enforced and continuously reapplied, while Group Policy Preferences instead configure an initial value, like a mapped drive, that the user can subsequently change and aren't strictly re-enforced the same way — both live in the same console and both flow through the same processing order, but behave very differently once applied. And where a single domain-wide password policy isn't precise enough, Fine-Grained Password Policies, using Password Settings Objects (PSOs), let different password and lockout rules apply to specific users or groups within that one domain — commonly paired with Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) so that service accounts can follow a stricter, separate policy without needing an entirely separate domain just for them. A Read-Only Domain Controller (RODC) is the natural fit for a branch office with weaker physical security — it caches credentials only for accounts permitted by its Password Replication Policy, so a stolen RODC only exposes what it was actually allowed to cache, not the whole domain's credentials. When an object gets deleted, the AD Recycle Bin restores it with essentially all of its original attributes, including group memberships, directly and quickly, a real improvement over the older tombstone reanimation method. And a gMSA provides one identity, shared across several servers like a load-balanced IIS farm, with automatic password rotation managed entirely by AD — something a standalone, single-server managed service account simply can't do. Finally, in a hybrid environment, Microsoft Entra Connect offers the same three sign-in choices covered for identity design generally: Password Hash Synchronization (PHS) syncs a hash of the password hash to Entra ID so sign-in keeps working through a brief on-premises outage — and never transmits a recoverable, plaintext password to the cloud — Pass-through Authentication (PTA) validates against on-premises AD in real time through an agent, and Federation (AD FS) hands authentication off entirely to an on-premises federation service.
