lessons.fundamentals:
Think of the FSMO roles like specialized jobs in a small town rather than a single mayor who does everything: one office issues birth certificates (Schema Master, forest-wide), another handles the town's master calendar for time-sensitive business (PDC Emulator) — spreading irreplaceable duties out instead of concentrating them all in one place that could vanish at once. A Read-Only Domain Controller is like giving a branch office a copy of the customer database with everyone's sensitive account numbers blacked out except the handful of customers that branch actually needs to serve — if that branch office's copy gets stolen, the thief only gets what was deliberately left visible.

GPO precedence with Enforced and Block Inheritance is like a company dress code: normally, the most specific department's rule (the OU) overrides the general company-wide rule, since the closest, most specific instruction usually wins. But if corporate stamps a rule 'mandatory, no exceptions' (Enforced), that rule applies even to a department that's otherwise been told it doesn't have to follow anything from above (Block Inheritance) — a blanket refusal to listen doesn't work against an order specifically marked as non-negotiable.
commonTraps: Enforced on a GPO overrides Block Inheritance — a child OU marked Block Inheritance still receives an Enforced GPO from above; enforcement beats blocking, not the other way around.
Password Hash Synchronization never sends a recoverable, plaintext password to Microsoft Entra ID — only a hash of the on-premises password hash.
A forest trust is transitive across two whole forests, but that transitivity doesn't extend to a third forest just because one of the trusted forests separately trusts it.
Raising a domain or forest functional level is one-way — it permanently rules out adding an older-OS domain controller afterward, so retiring the oldest DCs has to happen first.
lessons.scenario: A company is consolidating two newly merged subsidiaries' Active Directory forests and modernizing its domain controller footprint. It configures a forest trust so every domain in either forest can authenticate to the other automatically, and confirms neither forest's trust with a third, unrelated partner forest extends through that new relationship. Before raising its own forest functional level to unlock the AD Recycle Bin, it retires its last Windows Server 2012 domain controllers, since the level can never come back down once raised. At its branch offices, it deploys RODCs with a tightly scoped Password Replication Policy, so a stolen branch server only exposes the credentials it was actually allowed to cache. Its four-node load-balanced application farm now runs under a single gMSA instead of a hand-synchronized service account password, and its cloud sign-in is configured for Password Hash Synchronization, so authentication keeps working even during a brief on-premises outage — without ever running an AD FS server farm.
lessons.onTheJob: Losing a PDC Emulator with no working backup is exactly the kind of 2am page that turns 'seize the FSMO role' from a textbook phrase into something you're actually typing under pressure, usually while also fielding a help-desk flood about users who suddenly can't sign in. Raising a domain functional level looks like a routine checkbox until someone remembers there's still a Windows Server 2012 DC quietly running a legacy line-of-business app in a forgotten corner of the network, and that one-way decision suddenly needs a much longer conversation. GPO troubleshooting eats an outsized share of real admin time precisely because 'Enforced beats Block Inheritance' is the kind of rule everyone learns for the exam and then forgets the first time a setting mysteriously overrides what a department insisted they'd locked down. That same PHS/PTA/Federation decision reappears on SC-300 under Microsoft Entra Connect sync methods: Password Hash Sync, Pass-through Authentication, and Federation, just viewed from the identity-governance side instead of the infrastructure side — AZ-802 and SC-300 are really testing the same on-premises-to-cloud identity bridge from two different angles.

lessons.title: Hybrid Management, Clustering & Virtualization
lessons.summary: Bringing on-premises servers under Azure management with Arc, patching and protecting failover clusters, and the Hyper-V VM and container fundamentals underneath them.
lessons.reading:
Bringing an on-premises server under Azure's management plane doesn't require moving it anywhere. Azure Arc-enabled servers projects a server — on-premises or in another cloud — into Azure Resource Manager via the Connected Machine agent, without migrating the actual workload at all; once projected, that server can have Azure Policy, Azure Monitor, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, and Update Manager applied to it exactly like a native Azure VM, even though the compute itself never leaves the datacenter. Day-to-day, Windows Admin Center (WAC) gives administrators a free, modern, browser-based portal for managing servers locally or remotely — including Server Core installations with no local desktop shell at all — installed as a gateway rather than a separate console application every admin needs on their own workstation, and it extends with feature extensions like Azure Arc integration to bridge into that same cloud management plane from the same interface.

Once several servers are grouped into a failover cluster, keeping them patched without taking the whole cluster offline calls for Cluster-Aware Updating (CAU): it automates installing updates across every node one at a time, draining that node's workloads to the other nodes before patching and rebooting it, then bringing it back before moving on to the next node — running against a remote, CAU-enabled cluster on a schedule with no dedicated CAU role required, or in a self-updating mode where the cluster updates itself. A cluster only stays online while a majority of its configured votes are present, so its quorum model matters as much as its patching process: Node Majority gives one vote per node, the natural fit for an odd node count, while Node and File Share Majority or Node and Disk Majority add one extra vote from a witness so an even node count can still form a majority. Cloud Witness uses Azure Blob Storage as that witness instead — a common pick for a two-node cluster split across two small sites with no convenient third site to host a traditional file-share witness, since it needs only a small Azure Storage account rather than a full VM or site. None of this is safe to skip validating first, either: cluster validation (Test-Cluster) checks that nodes, storage, and networking meet Microsoft's requirements before a cluster is created, and running it again after changes confirms the cluster still meets them — a cluster built while skipping or failing validation is explicitly unsupported if a validation-related issue later causes an outage.

For moving or protecting individual VMs, three tools solve three different problems, and mixing them up is a common exam trap. Live Migration moves a running VM between Hyper-V hosts with zero perceptible downtime, needing shared or replicated storage (or SMB 3.0) plus compatible processors — the right call for planned host maintenance on a business-critical VM. Storage Migration moves a VM's actual virtual disks to different storage without changing hosts or causing downtime. Hyper-V Replica is different again: it asynchronously replicates a running VM's changes from a primary host to a replica host, on-premises or at another site, on an interval as low as 30 seconds, for disaster recovery rather than routine load balancing or maintenance — its replica VM sits offline until an actual failover happens, and a planned failover ahead of scheduled maintenance can move to the replica with zero data loss and automatically flip the original primary into the new replica role afterward. Separately, Storage Migration Service handles a different job entirely: migrating files, shares, and their security settings from an old file server to a new one, optionally transferring the old server's own name and IP address afterward so clients keep using the same UNC path with no reconfiguration at all — and it can inventory and migrate from Windows Server versions as far back as 2003, and even some NAS devices.

Underneath any of this, the VM and container choices you make at creation time are permanent. Generation 1 VMs emulate legacy BIOS hardware for maximum OS compatibility; Generation 2 VMs use UEFI firmware and support Secure Boot, and are required if a VM needs to boot from a virtual hard disk larger than 2 TB using GPT partitioning — but a VM's generation can't be changed after creation, so choosing wrong means recreating it, not converting it. A Hyper-V virtual switch is External (bound to a physical NIC, reaching the physical network), Internal (VMs and the host talk to each other, not the physical network), or Private (VMs on the same host talk only to each other, isolated even from the host) — the right pick for an isolated test network where VMs must never reach production or even the host OS. Checkpoints split similarly: a standard checkpoint captures memory and device state like a saved game, fast but not application-aware, while a production checkpoint uses Volume Shadow Copy Service inside the guest for an application-consistent copy — the only one safe to use routinely against something like a domain controller VM. And for containers, process isolation shares the host's kernel directly for the lowest overhead, while Hyper-V isolation runs each container inside its own lightweight utility VM with its own kernel instance, trading some overhead for VM-grade isolation — the right call for mutually distrusting tenants on the same host, or when a container's base image doesn't exactly match the host's kernel version.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to hybrid management and clustering? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals:
Azure Arc is like giving a corporate office a security badge and a spot on the company directory for a satellite office that never actually moves buildings — the satellite office still physically sits where it always has, but now shows up in the same directory, follows the same company policies, and gets the same centralized alerts as every other office. Cluster quorum is like a company board that only conducts business with a majority of members present — an odd-numbered board can always find a majority among just its own members, but an even-numbered board keeps a tie-breaking advisor (the witness) on retainer specifically so a split vote never happens.

Live Migration, Storage Migration, and Hyper-V Replica are like three different ways to handle a shop that's outgrowing its building. Live Migration is moving the whole running shop into a new building overnight with the lights never going off. Storage Migration is keeping the shop exactly where it is but moving all its inventory to a bigger stockroom. Hyper-V Replica is keeping a second, fully-stocked shop quietly ready in another town, just in case the first one ever has to close its doors unexpectedly.
commonTraps: Hyper-V Replica is a disaster-recovery tool, not a live-migration substitute — its replica VM stays offline until an actual failover, unlike Live Migration's zero-downtime move of a running VM.
A cluster's own quorum witness matters even in a two-node cluster split across sites — Cloud Witness uses a small Azure Storage account instead of needing a full third physical site.

Skipping cluster validation isn't a supported shortcut just because the cluster comes online — Microsoft calls a cluster built that way unsupported if a validation-related issue later causes an outage.
A VM's generation can't be changed after creation — picking Generation 1 when Secure Boot or a boot disk over 2 TB is needed means recreating the VM, not converting it.
lessons.scenario: A retailer is consolidating two branch-office Hyper-V hosts into a proper hybrid-managed environment. It Arc-enables both hosts so central IT can apply Azure Policy and Azure Monitor alerting to them without moving any workload into Azure, and manages them day to day through Windows Admin Center instead of RDP, since several of the underlying servers run Server Core. It builds a six-node failover cluster at its main site, patched monthly through Cluster-Aware Updating so no single maintenance window takes the whole cluster offline, and — since a second cluster spans two small branch offices with no third site available — configures Cloud Witness rather than a traditional file-share witness. Before either cluster goes into production, cluster validation confirms the nodes, storage, and networking actually meet Microsoft's requirements. For its most critical VM, it uses Live Migration ahead of planned host maintenance for zero downtime, while a separate Hyper-V Replica configuration keeps a disaster-recovery copy quietly running at a secondary site in case the whole primary site is ever lost.
lessons.onTheJob: Cluster-Aware Updating sounds fully automated in the documentation, but a real Patch Tuesday still means babysitting the rolling reboot to catch the one node that doesn't drain its workloads cleanly before the next round of updates lands. Cloud Witness gets adopted less out of architectural elegance and more because someone's two-site cluster failed a quorum vote during a real outage, and the postmortem made 'we need a tie-breaking vote from somewhere' impossible to ignore. Mixing up Live Migration and Hyper-V Replica during an actual host failure is a genuinely common on-call mistake — reaching for the wrong tool costs precious minutes before someone remembers that a replica sitting offline needs an actual failover, not a live move. A live migration that stalls or fails partway through even with Processor Compatibility Mode enabled is a common surprise the first time hosts get upgraded piecemeal across a hardware refresh, since PCM only masks specific instruction-set differences and doesn't guarantee a clean migration across every generation gap between old and new host CPUs.

lessons.title: On-Premises & Hybrid Networking
lessons.summary: DNS zone types, DHCP high availability, IP address management, and connecting on-premises networks to Azure and RADIUS-authenticated access.
lessons.reading:
DNS in a Windows Server environment comes in a few zone types that solve different problems. A primary zone holds the writable, authoritative copy of a zone's records. A secondary zone holds a read-only copy, kept current through a zone transfer from a primary. A stub zone holds only NS, SOA, and glue A/AAAA records — just enough to find the authoritative servers for a namespace, not a resolvable copy of the records themselves, which is exactly why it's so much lighter than a full secondary zone: it's a referral shortcut, not a copy of the data. An AD-integrated zone instead stores its data directly in Active Directory, gaining automatic multi-master replication to every domain controller and support for secure dynamic updates restricted to authenticated computers — the natural pick whenever a scenario specifically wants secure, automatic replication to every DC rather than manually configured zone transfers.

DHCP high availability offers two different failover modes depending on what you're actually trying to achieve. Load balance mode has both DHCP servers actively answering client requests, splitting the load between them by a configured percentage — an 80/20 split favoring a datacenter server still means the branch server actively answers roughly a fifth of requests under normal conditions, not zero. Hot standby mode instead designates one server as fully active and the other as a passive backup that only starts answering if the active server becomes unavailable — the natural fit for a branch office, where a central DHCP server normally handles everything and a local server only takes over if the WAN link to the central site drops.

Managing DNS and DHCP at scale, especially once there are many servers and scopes, is what IP Address Management (IPAM) is built for: a Windows Server role that discovers, monitors, and centrally manages DHCP and DNS servers and their IP address space from one console, including tracking utilization and flagging overlapping or duplicate scopes across the whole environment. IPAM doesn't replace those roles, though — it manages existing DHCP and DNS servers from one place, and installing it doesn't remove the need to actually deploy those roles somewhere in the first place.

Connecting a network to Azure, or authenticating access onto it, has its own two decisions. A Site-to-Site VPN connects an on-premises network to Azure over the public internet using encrypted tunnels — cheaper and quicker to stand up, but subject to internet variability. ExpressRoute instead uses a private, dedicated circuit through a connectivity provider, bypassing the public internet entirely for more predictable latency and higher available bandwidth, at a higher cost — the answer whenever predictable latency and available bandwidth matter more than cost. And for centralizing authentication onto the network itself, Network Policy Server (NPS) is Microsoft's RADIUS server and proxy implementation, centralizing authentication, authorization, and accounting for VPN connections, 802.1X wired or wireless access, and other RADIUS-aware devices from one shared policy engine — though NPS itself doesn't terminate the VPN connection; RRAS or a third-party VPN device does that and simply forwards the authentication request to NPS as the RADIUS server.

lessons.fundamentals: A stub zone is like keeping only a forwarding address for a department that moved to another building, instead of keeping a full copy of everyone in that department's files — enough to know exactly where to send an inquiry, without carrying the overhead of an entire duplicate filing cabinet. DHCP hot standby is like a backup cashier who stands off to the side doing nothing until the main register goes down, at which point they step in immediately — load balance mode is more like two cashiers both actively ringing up customers side by side the whole time, just with one handling more of the line than the other.
commonTraps: A stub zone only holds NS/SOA/glue records to find the authoritative servers — it isn't a resolvable copy of the zone's actual records the way a secondary zone is.
DHCP load balance mode still has both servers actively answering requests, just split by a configured percentage — hot standby is the mode where one server does nothing until the other fails.
IPAM manages existing DHCP and DNS server roles from one console — it isn't itself a DHCP or DNS server, and deploying it doesn't remove the need to run those roles somewhere.
NPS doesn't terminate a VPN connection itself — RRAS (or a third-party VPN device) does that and forwards the authentication request to NPS as the RADIUS server.
lessons.scenario: A company with a central datacenter and several branch offices is redesigning its on-premises networking. Its DNS zone is AD-integrated, so records replicate automatically and securely to every domain controller without manually configured zone transfers, while a stub zone points to a partner company's authoritative servers for a namespace it needs to resolve but not host. DHCP runs in load balance mode with an 80/20 split favoring the datacenter server for normal capacity, while a separate branch office specifically uses hot standby, since its local server should stay passive unless the WAN link to the datacenter actually drops. IPAM gives the networking team one console to spot an overlapping DHCP scope before it causes a conflict. For its latency-sensitive hybrid application, the company chooses ExpressRoute over a Site-to-Site VPN, since predictable latency and available bandwidth matter more than the extra cost, and deploys NPS as a single RADIUS policy engine authenticating both 802.1X wired switch ports and remote VPN connections from one place.
lessons.onTheJob: A stub zone versus a full secondary zone rarely gets debated in the abstract — it usually comes up when someone notices unnecessary zone-transfer traffic crossing a slow WAN link and traces it back to a zone that only ever needed a referral, not a full copy of the records. DHCP failover mode misconfigurations are a classic branch-office ticket: an 80/20 load-balance split meant to favor the datacenter server quietly leaves a branch server actively answering a fifth of requests nobody accounted for in capacity planning. NPS as a single RADIUS policy engine looks tidy in a design doc, but the on-call reality is that when it goes down, VPN, wireless, and switch-port authentication can all fail at once, which is why it usually ends up more redundant in production than the original diagram showed.

lessons.title: Storage & File Services
lessons.summary: Unifying and replicating file shares, pooling local disks with Storage Spaces and S2D, reclaiming space, and the file systems and block-storage options underneath.
lessons.reading:
Two related but distinct technologies solve the "many file servers, one experience" problem. DFS Namespaces (DFS-N) presents a single logical folder path, like \\contoso\shares, that transparently points users to shared folders spread across one or more actual servers, regardless of which physical server actually holds a given folder. DFS Replication (DFS-R) is the piece that keeps the real folder contents synchronized between multiple servers, so any of them can serve current data — the two are commonly deployed together, DFS-R keeping the copies in sync while DFS-N gives users one consistent path that resolves to whichever in-sync copy is closest or available, but each can be deployed on its own, and neither is the same thing as Storage Replica's block-level replication.

Pooling local disks together is Storage Spaces' job, and its resiliency types trade fault tolerance against performance and storage efficiency. Simple striping spreads data with no redundancy at all — fastest, but zero fault tolerance. A two-way (or three-way) mirror duplicates data across disks, tolerating one (or two) disk failures with strong write performance. Parity spreads data plus parity information, more storage-efficient than mirroring for equivalent fault tolerance, but at the cost of slower random writes — a better fit for larger, less write-intensive data like backups or archives than a busy transactional workload. Storage Spaces Direct (S2D) takes this further by pooling local, direct-attached storage across every node of a failover cluster into one software-defined, cluster-wide storage pool, enabling hyperconverged infrastructure with no separate SAN — but S2D still needs a genuinely functioning failover cluster underneath it, so the same quorum models and witness types that govern any other cluster still apply here too, and a shared, cluster-wide namespace for that pooled storage is what actually lets every node read and write to it simultaneously without dismounting and remounting disks.

Two more features manage what's already sitting on disk. Data Deduplication is a post-process, file-system-level feature that finds and eliminates duplicate chunks of data, replacing repeats with references to a single stored copy — a strong fit for general file shares, VDI libraries, and backup targets, but a poor one for heavily and randomly modified files like a live database, where duplicate chunks are rare and the processing overhead isn't worth it. And the file system underneath any of this matters, too: ReFS (Resilient File System) prioritizes resiliency and scalability for large data volumes, using checksums and automatic corruption repair when paired with mirrored or parity Storage Spaces, but it is not supported as a boot volume — NTFS remains the general-purpose default and is required for the Windows Server system volume, with ReFS reserved for data volumes where its self-healing can actually do something useful.

For data that needs to leave the building, or be reached without a full file-share stack, a few more options round this out. Azure File Sync keeps an on-premises Windows Server file share synchronized with an Azure file share, and can enable cloud tiering, so infrequently used files are replaced locally with a pointer while their full content stays safely in Azure, streamed back on access — from a user's perspective the file is still just "there," just retrieved on demand once it's actually opened. Storage Replica provides block-level, volume-to-volume replication independent of whatever file system sits on top, with synchronous replication guaranteeing zero data loss (at the cost of needing low latency between sites) and asynchronous replication tolerating higher latency in exchange for a small, non-zero possible data-loss window. And an iSCSI Target Server presents block-level storage over the network as an iSCSI target, letting a client connect to it as if it were a local disk — a genuinely different sharing model than DFS's file-level folders, useful when an application, like a specific SQL Server database, needs its own raw block device rather than a network file share.

lessons.fundamentals: DFS Namespaces and DFS Replication are like a company's shared mail-forwarding address and its actual mail-sorting operation: DFS-N is the single forwarding address everyone uses no matter which back-office branch actually processes their mail, and DFS-R is the process that makes sure every branch has the same up-to-date mail regardless of which one you ask. Storage Spaces resiliency types are like choosing how many copies of a photo album to keep: no copies at all is fastest to create but you lose everything if one album is damaged (striping); an identical duplicate album (mirroring) survives losing one copy but takes twice the shelf space; and a shared index that can reconstruct a missing page from the others (parity) saves shelf space but takes longer to update whenever a page changes.
commonTraps: Data Deduplication is a poor fit for heavily, randomly modified files like a live database — it shines on general file shares, VDI libraries, and backup targets instead.
ReFS is not supported as a Windows Server boot volume — NTFS is still required there; ReFS is for data volumes, ideally backed by mirrored or parity Storage Spaces.
Storage Spaces Direct still needs a genuinely functioning failover cluster underneath it — it's a storage feature layered on clustering, not a replacement for it.

Storage Replica works at the block level below the file system, so it doesn't care what kind of data is on the volume — that's different from DFS Replication, which specifically synchronizes file-share contents.
lessons.scenario: A company is modernizing its file services across a datacenter and several branch offices. Users across three file servers now reach their files through a single DFS-N path, with DFS-R keeping the underlying folder contents synchronized in near real time between two of those servers for resilience. Its new hyperconverged Hyper-V cluster pools local NVMe disks with Storage Spaces Direct, formatted with ReFS so background bit-rot corruption gets detected and repaired automatically without taking the volume offline, while an older, less write-intensive archive server gets Data Deduplication turned on to reclaim disk space with minimal risk. A branch office file server with limited local disk uses Azure File Sync with cloud tiering enabled, so rarely touched files still appear in the folder structure but stream back from Azure only when actually opened. And a finance application that needs its own raw block device, not a network share, connects to an iSCSI Target Server instead.
lessons.onTheJob: DFS-R replication delays are the quiet cause behind a surprising number of 'the file I just saved from another office isn't showing up yet' tickets, and diagnosing them usually means checking replication backlog before assuming something is actually broken. Turning on Data Deduplication against what looks like a routine file share sometimes gets applied a little too enthusiastically to a volume that turns out to host a database file, and the resulting performance complaint is how a lot of admins learn where dedup genuinely doesn't belong. Storage Spaces Direct sounds like it eliminates SAN headaches entirely, but the underlying failover cluster still has all the same quorum and validation requirements as any other cluster, which is easy to forget until a two-node S2D cluster goes down over a quorum issue nobody planned for. ReFS's self-healing also only actually fires when the volume sits on a resilient Storage Spaces layout that can supply a good copy to repair from — a ReFS volume placed on a simple, non-redundant space looks identical on the surface but silently loses that automatic corruption-repair capability, which usually only gets discovered the first time a checksum mismatch turns into data loss instead of a quiet repair.

lessons.title: Securing Windows Server Hybrid Infrastructure
lessons.summary: Application control, protecting credentials in memory and at rest, restricting how privileged accounts can authenticate, and detecting attacks against on-premises identity.
lessons.reading:
Stopping unapproved code from running at all starts with choosing between two allowlisting technologies that work at very different levels. Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) enforces a code-integrity policy evaluated by the kernel itself and applied system-wide, determining what's allowed to run before it even starts — critically, that enforcement survives even if a local administrator account on the box is later compromised, since it isn't a user-mode control an elevated attacker could simply disable. AppLocker, by contrast, is a rule-based allowlisting feature running at the user-mode level, which can apply different rules per user or group, but is correspondingly easier to bypass than a kernel-enforced WDAC policy. A requirement for enforcement that survives a compromised local administrator account, applied before any unapproved binary can even start, points specifically to WDAC.

Protecting the secrets already in memory is a separate problem from controlling what runs. Credential Guard uses virtualization-based security (VBS) to isolate the LSASS process and NTLM/Kerberos secrets inside a protected, hypervisor-enforced container, so that even an administrator on the host, or malware with kernel-level access, can't extract them with a tool like Mimikatz. It needs hardware virtualization support to work at all, and it specifically blocks storing reversibly-encrypted passwords and unconstrained Kerberos delegation — which is exactly why it sometimes breaks a specific legacy authentication scenario that depended on one of those.

Two more tools manage privileged access itself rather than the secrets sitting in memory. Windows LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) automatically rotates and stores the password for a local administrator account on each domain-joined, or Microsoft Entra-joined, computer — in Active Directory or in Microsoft Entra ID — with retrieval controlled by delegated permissions, so a helpdesk technician can look up the current password to troubleshoot a specific machine without ever having set or memorized it themselves. Just Enough Administration (JEA) solves an adjacent but different problem: it lets an organization grant a support technician access to run a specific, limited set of PowerShell cmdlets under an elevated identity, without handing that technician full local administrator rights on the server at all.

Some protections apply to specific high-value accounts directly. Adding an account to the Protected Users security group blocks it from authenticating with NTLM, DES, or RC4 encryption, prevents credential caching, and disables delegation of its credentials, forcing Kerberos with stronger encryption only — with no fallback available, so an application or device that only supports NTLM will simply fail to authenticate that account rather than falling back gracefully. And for detecting an attack already underway against on-premises identity specifically, Microsoft Defender for Identity is a cloud service that monitors on-premises AD DS, through sensors installed on domain controllers, for signs of compromise like reconnaissance, pass-the-hash, DCSync attempts, or golden ticket usage — surfacing those alerts alongside other Microsoft Defender XDR signals, which is what makes it possible to correlate an on-premises AD attack with cloud workload signals in one unified security view.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to Windows Server hardening? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: WDAC and AppLocker are like two different levels of building security: WDAC is a locked, guarded entrance that checks every single person against a master list before they're even let into the lobby, run by security staff nobody in the building can override — even a building manager can't just wave someone through. AppLocker is more like a sign-in sheet at each individual floor's reception desk, which a determined visitor could talk their way around more easily. Windows LAPS is like a hotel's key-card system automatically changing every room's lock combination after each guest checks out, so staff can issue a working key on request without ever needing to remember or reuse yesterday's code.
commonTraps: WDAC enforcement happens at the kernel level and survives a compromised local administrator account — AppLocker's user-mode rules are easier for an elevated attacker to work around.

Credential Guard specifically blocks storing reversibly-encrypted passwords and unconstrained Kerberos delegation — which is exactly why it can break a legacy authentication setup that depended on either one.
An account in the Protected Users group has no NTLM fallback at all — if Kerberos is briefly unavailable, authentication simply fails rather than falling back.
Microsoft Defender for Identity watches the on-premises identity plane specifically — it's a different signal source from Entra ID Identity Protection, which focuses on cloud sign-ins.
lessons.scenario: A regulated company hardens a fleet of file servers and its most sensitive administrative accounts. It deploys WDAC in enforced mode on the file servers, so unapproved executables can't run even if an attacker later gains local administrator rights on one of them. Every server's local administrator password is now managed by Windows LAPS, rotated automatically and retrievable only through delegated permissions, while day-to-day troubleshooting access for the helpdesk goes through JEA instead of full administrator rights. Domain admin accounts are placed in the Protected Users group, forcing Kerberos-only authentication with no NTLM fallback, and every domain controller runs a Credential Guard-protected LSASS process so a compromised local administrator on the box still can't extract cached credentials with a tool like Mimikatz. Microsoft Defender for Identity sensors on those same domain controllers feed alerts — reconnaissance, pass-the-hash attempts — into the same security operations view as the company's cloud workload signals, giving the security team one correlated picture instead of two separate ones.
lessons.onTheJob: Deploying WDAC in enforced mode is one of those changes that looks purely defensive on paper and then breaks a legacy in-house tool nobody documented, which is why real rollouts almost always start in audit mode first rather than going straight to enforcement. Credential Guard's block on unconstrained Kerberos delegation and reversibly-encrypted passwords is a genuinely common source of 'why did this one legacy app just stop authenticating' tickets after a hardening pass, and tracking that down usually eats a whole afternoon the first time it happens. Windows LAPS adoption is often driven less by a security mandate and more by a help-desk team simply tired of a shared, stale local admin password everyone half-remembers and nobody's confident is actually secure anymore.

lessons.title: Monitoring & Troubleshooting Windows Server
lessons.summary: Local performance counters and event logs, unifying monitoring across a hybrid fleet with Azure Monitor, and patch compliance with Azure Update Manager.
lessons.reading:
Locally, Performance Monitor displays real-time or logged performance counters — CPU, memory, disk queue length, and so on — but capturing the same set of counters consistently over time, rather than reconfiguring the tool fresh every time an issue comes up, is what a Data Collector Set is for: it groups counters, trace data, and configuration into a single, reusable, schedulable collection job, and can even be configured to trigger an alert or run a task when a counter crosses a defined threshold, turning raw performance data into a proactive signal instead of a report someone has to remember to go read.

Scaling that same idea across a hybrid fleet of both native Azure VMs and on-premises servers is Azure Monitor Agent's (AMA) job: it's the single, unified agent installed on all of them, replacing the older Log Analytics (MMA/OMS) agent, and a Data Collection Rule (DCR) defines exactly what that agent collects, any transformation applied to it, and which destination — typically a Log Analytics workspace — it's sent to. One DCR can be associated with many machines at once, which is exactly what lets a single collection configuration apply consistently across a whole fleet instead of being authored separately for every server.

Once that data is actually flowing into a Log Analytics workspace, it's queried with Kusto Query Language (KQL), a read-only language built around piping data through a chain of operators — like where, summarize, and project — to filter and shape results. A KQL query that flags a problem interactively can usually be turned directly into an automated log alert rule with very little extra work, and it's worth keeping the two kinds of Azure Monitor alert rules straight: a metric alert evaluates a numeric signal, like CPU percentage, against a threshold on a schedule, while a log alert runs a KQL query on a schedule instead and fires based on its results. Either kind of alert rule is deliberately kept separate from the action group that defines what actually happens when it fires — an email, an SMS, a webhook, or an Azure Automation runbook — precisely so the same action group, say, paging the on-call team, can be reused across many different, unrelated alert rules rather than being redefined inside each one.

Windows Admin Center brings a slice of this experience directly into a browser without switching tools: it shows real-time and historical performance data for a managed server, and its Azure Monitor extension can forward that data to Log Analytics and configure alert rules from the very same interface. Azure Update Manager centralizes patch compliance and scheduled update installation across both Azure VMs and Azure Arc-enabled on-premises servers from one place in the Azure portal — but a server has to actually be Arc-enabled, or be a native Azure VM, before Update Manager can see or patch it at all; Arc-enabling a server alone isn't enough if the Arc extension or agent configuration that actually reports update data is still missing. And when something's already gone wrong, Reliability Monitor is the right first stop: it plots a rolling stability index over time and correlates it with specific events like installs, crashes, or updates, making it easy to spot exactly when a problem started — after which Event Viewer's full, detailed, filterable event logs (System, Application, Security, and role-specific logs) are what actually confirm the root cause.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to Windows Server monitoring? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals:
A Data Collector Set is like setting a recurring calendar reminder to take the same vital-sign readings every morning, instead of only checking them the one time something already feels wrong — the value is in having a consistent history to compare against. Separating an alert rule from its action group is like separating a smoke detector (the condition that triggers) from the phone tree it calls (the response) — the same phone tree can be wired up to a smoke detector in the kitchen and a separate one in the garage, without redefining who gets called each time.

Reliability Monitor and Event Viewer are like a hospital's vital-signs chart and its detailed medical chart: the vital-signs chart quickly shows you exactly when a patient's condition started declining, and the detailed chart is where you actually dig in afterward to find out precisely what happened.
commonTraps: A metric alert evaluates a numeric threshold on a schedule; a log alert runs a KQL query on a schedule instead — picking the wrong one for a fast CPU-spike alert versus a complex investigation is a common mix-up.
An alert rule and its action group are separate on purpose — the same action group (like paging on-call) can be reused across many unrelated alert rules instead of being redefined in each one.

Arc-enabling a server alone doesn't make it visible to Azure Update Manager — it still needs to actually be reporting update data through Arc (or be a native Azure VM) before Update Manager can assess or patch it.
Reliability Monitor is the fast first stop for spotting when a problem started — Event Viewer's detailed, filterable logs are what actually confirm the root cause afterward.
lessons.scenario: An operations team supporting a hybrid fleet of Azure VMs and on-premises servers standardizes its monitoring. Every server gets a Data Collector Set capturing the same CPU, memory, and disk counters on a schedule, feeding into Azure Monitor Agent, deployed consistently across the whole fleet through a single Data Collection Rule rather than one written per machine. Their Log Analytics workspace holds it all, queried with KQL for deep investigation, while a fast metric alert pages the on-call engineer within a minute of any server's CPU spiking — reusing the exact same action group that a separate log alert, watching for a specific error pattern, also fires into. Windows Admin Center gives an on-call engineer the same real-time view in a browser without switching to the Azure portal, and Azure Update Manager reports patch compliance across the fleet — though one batch of newly Arc-enabled servers shows up with no update data at all, until the team realizes the Arc extension needed to actually report that data was never configured. When a server starts crashing intermittently, Reliability Monitor's timeline quickly shows exactly when the trouble started, right before a new driver update — and Event Viewer's detailed logs confirm that driver as the actual cause.
lessons.onTheJob: A Data Collection Rule that quietly stops reporting for one server in a fleet is a genuinely common source of a monitoring blind spot nobody notices until an incident happens on exactly that machine, which is why real teams periodically audit DCR coverage instead of trusting it was configured once and forgotten. Finding out that Arc-enabling a server alone doesn't make it visible to Update Manager is the kind of thing admins usually discover the hard way, staring at a patch compliance report with a batch of servers mysteriously missing instead of reading the fine print first. Reliability Monitor's timeline is underused in practice, mostly because admins jump straight to Event Viewer's noisy logs out of habit — the fast win of spotting exactly when a driver update correlates with new instability gets skipped more often than it should.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: You have 120 minutes for 60 questions — about 2.0 minutes each on average. Budget more time for multi-part scenario questions and less for straight recall, rather than pacing every question identically.
Real scoring isn't a flat percentage of questions right (some count for more than others) — treat 70%+ as a safe buffer to aim for, not an exact threshold to just clear.

Flag anything you're unsure of and move on rather than stalling — a question later in the exam can sometimes jog a detail you needed earlier, and you get partial credit for nothing by running out of time on one question.
On multi-select ('choose N') questions, eliminate the options you're confident are wrong first; guessing among 2 plausible answers beats guessing among 4.
Your first read of a question is usually right — change an answer only when you find a specific detail you missed, not from general second-guessing.

cheatSheet.heading: AD DS & hybrid identity essentials
points: Five FSMO roles total: Schema Master and Domain Naming Master are forest-wide (one each per forest); RID Master, PDC Emulator, and Infrastructure Master are domain-wide (one each per domain).

Microsoft Entra Connect sync methods: Password Hash Sync (PHS) is simplest and most resilient, Pass-through Authentication (PTA) needs on-prem agents to stay online for every sign-in, and Federation (AD FS) is the most complex, rarely the right answer unless a specific requirement forces it.
The Infrastructure Master only matters in a multi-domain forest where the Global Catalog is not on every DC — otherwise it does nothing.
AD Recycle Bin needs forest functional level Windows Server 2008 R2 or higher and must be manually enabled — it isn't on by default.
A Read-Only Domain Controller (RODC) doesn't cache any account's password unless that account is explicitly added to its Password Replication Policy allow list.

cheatSheet.heading: Hyper-V & Storage Spaces Direct
points: Generation 2 VMs support UEFI, Secure Boot, and larger boot volumes; Generation 1 exists mainly for older or 32-bit guest OSes.
Production checkpoints use VSS/file-system consistency and are safe for production workloads; Standard checkpoints also save memory/device state but are dev/test only.
Storage Spaces Direct needs a minimum of 2 nodes (a 2-node cluster needs a witness) and scales up to 16 nodes.

Two-way mirror behaves like RAID-1 and survives one node/drive failure; three-way mirror needs 3+ nodes and survives two failures; parity trades resiliency overhead for better usable capacity but costs more CPU.
Storage Replica synchronous mode gives zero data loss but needs low latency between sites; asynchronous mode tolerates higher latency but can lose in-flight data on failover.

cheatSheet.heading: Windows Server networking (DNS/DHCP/VPN)
points: A conditional forwarder sends queries for a specific namespace to specific DNS servers; a stub zone stores only that zone's NS/SOA/glue records and refreshes them automatically.
AD-integrated zones replicate via AD (multi-master); standard Primary/Secondary zones use one-way zone transfers from the primary to each secondary.
DHCP failover has two modes: Hot standby (one server active, one passive backup) and Load balance (both serve requests, split by percentage).
Always On VPN is Microsoft's modern replacement for DirectAccess, which is being phased out.
Site-to-site VPN keeps two networks continuously connected; point-to-site VPN connects a single client machine to a network on demand.

cheatSheet.heading: Azure Arc-enabled server management
points: Arc-enabled servers projects a non-Azure (on-prem or other-cloud) machine into Azure Resource Manager as a resource — it does NOT migrate or move the server itself.
Onboarding installs the Connected Machine agent (azcmagent), which needs outbound connectivity to specific Azure endpoints or Azure Private Link.
Once Arc-enabled, a server can receive Azure Policy, Azure Monitor, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, and Update Manager coverage just like a native Azure VM.
Arc-enabled servers get a resource ID and resource group like any Azure resource, enabling the same RBAC and tagging as cloud-native VMs.

cheatSheet.heading: Windows Admin Center basics
points: Windows Admin Center is the modern, browser-based successor to many MMC snap-ins (Server Manager, Failover Cluster Manager, Disk Management), not a replacement for Active Directory Administrative Center.
It can run in gateway mode on a server managing many machines, or desktop mode on a Windows 10/11 client managing itself plus others it connects to.
WAC needs no Azure connection to manage local servers, but can optionally register with Azure for hybrid features like Azure Monitor and Azure Backup integration.
Extensions add functionality — for example Storage Migration Service or Azure Arc registration — beyond the built-in tools.

cheatSheet.heading: Security & patching
points: Microsoft Defender for Cloud's free tier gives Secure Score and basic recommendations; paid Defender plans (e.g. Defender for Servers) add features like just-in-time VM access and file integrity monitoring.
Azure Update Manager (successor to Azure Update Management) can patch both Azure VMs and Arc-enabled on-prem/multi-cloud servers from one place.
WSUS is still the traditional on-prem patch approval/distribution tool — Update Manager doesn't replace an existing WSUS deployment, it can work alongside or independently of it.
BitLocker requires a TPM (or a USB startup key as a workaround), and recovery keys should be backed up to AD DS or Entra ID, not left only on the local machine.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day reminders
points: AZ-802 assumes AZ-800-level knowledge — it now covers what used to be split across AZ-800 (core admin) and AZ-801 (advanced security), after those two exams were retired and consolidated.
Microsoft certification exams are typically scored 0–1000 with 700 required to pass, not a flat percentage.
Scenario questions often hinge on whether Entra ID/Azure is in scope at all — the 'right' tool depends on hybrid vs. on-prem-only requirements.
When two options both technically work, pick the one requiring the least new infrastructure/agents unless the scenario specifically asks for a security-hardening trade-off.

cliChallenges.prompt: Create a new Active Directory user named 'Jane Smith' with SamAccountName 'jsmith', and enable the account.
cliChallenges.explanation: New-ADUser creates the account disabled by default unless -Enabled $true is passed — a common cause of "why can't this new user log in" scenarios.

cliChallenges.prompt: Create a new global security group named 'Finance-Team'.
cliChallenges.explanation: -GroupScope (DomainLocal/Global/Universal) and -GroupCategory (Security/Distribution) are both required — AD won't infer either one.
-Identity takes the group, -Members takes one or more users/groups/computers to add to it — easy to mix up which side is which under exam pressure.

cliChallenges.prompt: Install the DNS Server role on the local server, including its management tools.
cliChallenges.explanation: -IncludeManagementTools is easy to forget — without it, the role installs but the matching MMC snap-in/PowerShell module doesn't come with it.

cliChallenges.prompt: Restart the local server immediately, forcing any running applications to close.
cliChallenges.explanation: Without -Force, Restart-Computer will prompt to confirm and won't force-close apps with unsaved state — an important distinction for scripted/unattended maintenance windows.

cliChallenges.prompt: Create a new Hyper-V virtual machine named 'VM-App02' with 4GB of memory, using generation 2.
cliChallenges.explanation: Generation 2 VMs support UEFI/Secure Boot and larger boot disks but need a compatible guest OS — Generation 1 is still required for some older OS images.

cliChallenges.prompt: Start the Hyper-V virtual machine named 'VM-App02'.
cliChallenges.explanation: Start-VM/Stop-VM are the Hyper-V host-level equivalents of powering a physical machine on/off — distinct from anything you'd run inside the guest OS itself.

cliChallenges.prompt: Configure network adapter 'Ethernet' with a static IP address 192.168.1.50, prefix length 24, and default gateway 192.168.1.1.
cliChallenges.explanation: -PrefixLength 24 is the modern equivalent of a 255.255.255.0 subnet mask — New-NetIPAddress is the PowerShell replacement for the older netsh interface commands.

cliChallenges.prompt: Set the DNS server addresses for network adapter 'Ethernet' to 10.0.0.4 and 10.0.0.5.
cliChallenges.explanation: -ServerAddresses takes a comma-separated list in priority order — the first address is queried first, with the rest as fallback.

cliChallenges.prompt: Format volume D as NTFS with the label 'Data', without a confirmation prompt.
cliChallenges.explanation: -Confirm:$false suppresses the interactive prompt that a destructive command like this shows by default — needed for unattended/scripted provisioning.

cliChallenges.prompt: Create a new Windows Firewall rule named 'Allow-HTTPS' that allows inbound TCP traffic on port 443.
cliChallenges.explanation: New-NetFirewallRule is the PowerShell equivalent of adding a rule in Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security — -Direction and -Action are both required or the rule is ambiguous.

cliChallenges.prompt: Retrieve the 20 most recent entries from the System event log.
cliChallenges.explanation: Get-WinEvent is the modern replacement for Get-EventLog and works with both classic and newer structured (ETW) event logs — -MaxEvents caps how many entries come back, newest first.

madlibs.scenario: Two companies merge, each with its own Active Directory forest, and need every domain in both forests to authenticate to the other automatically — that calls for a {b1}. Within a single one of those forests, a shortcut trust is later added between two distant child domains purely to shorten the {b2} that authentication requests would otherwise have to walk.

options: two-way forest trust
one-way external trust
realm trust
shortcut trust
referral path
password hash
Group Policy link
schema partition

madlibs.explanation: A forest trust is transitive across every domain in both forests, matching the merger's need for blanket authentication; an external trust is non-transitive and would need repeating per domain pair. A shortcut trust exists specifically to shorten the normal domain-tree referral path Kerberos would otherwise walk between two distant child domains already in the same forest.

madlibs.scenario: An administrator needs to move a running production VM to another host ahead of planned maintenance with zero perceptible downtime, given shared storage and compatible processors between the two hosts — that's {b1}. Separately, to keep an asynchronously up-to-date copy of that same VM at a secondary site in case the whole primary host is lost, they configure {b2}.

options: Live Migration
Hyper-V Replica
Storage Replica
Cluster-Aware Updating
Live Migration
Hyper-V Replica
Cluster-Aware Updating
Cloud Witness

madlibs.explanation: Live Migration moves a running VM between hosts with no perceptible downtime, given shared/compatible storage and processors. Hyper-V Replica instead keeps an asynchronous, periodically updated copy at a secondary site for disaster recovery — a different problem from a live, zero-downtime move between two hosts that are both currently healthy.

madlibs.scenario: Users need one unified path like \\contoso\shares that transparently maps to folders physically spread across three file servers — that's {b1}. To keep the actual file contents inside those folders synchronized between two of those servers, so either can serve current data, the administrator also configures {b2} underneath it.

options: DFS Namespaces
DFS Replication
Storage Spaces Direct
Data Deduplication
DFS Namespaces
DFS Replication
Cluster-Aware Updating
Azure File Sync

madlibs.explanation: DFS Namespaces provides the single unified logical path across multiple servers' shares. DFS Replication is the separate feature that actually synchronizes folder contents between servers — a namespace alone doesn't keep content in sync without replication configured underneath it.

madlibs.scenario: A hybrid administrator wants performance counters and Windows Event Log data collected the same way from both Azure VMs and on-premises servers, into one Log Analytics workspace, using collection logic authored once and applied to many machines at a time — that requires deploying the {b1} extension to each machine and associating it with a {b2}. Before an on-premises server can be targeted this way at all, it must first be Azure Arc-enabled.

options: Azure Monitor Agent (AMA)
legacy Log Analytics agent (MMA)
Dependency agent
Network Watcher agent
Data Collection Rule (DCR)
Recovery Services vault
Action Group
Automation runbook

madlibs.explanation: Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) is the current, unified agent for both Azure and Arc-enabled on-premises machines, replacing the legacy Log Analytics (MMA) agent. It's driven by a Data Collection Rule, which defines what to collect and where to send it once, then can be associated with many machines — a Recovery Services vault, Action Group, and Automation runbook all serve unrelated purposes (backup, alert routing, and scripted automation, respectively).

madlibs.scenario: A security team wants to let a small group of junior admins run only a specific, pre-approved set of PowerShell cmdlets on a server — including restarting a particular service — without granting them full local administrator rights. That narrowly scoped, role-based constrained PowerShell endpoint is {b1}. Separately, to guarantee a service account's password is unique, complex, and automatically rotated without any human ever needing to know or type it, they configure a {b2} instead of a traditional user account with a manually set password.

options: Just Enough Administration (JEA)
Just-In-Time (JIT) VM access
Windows LAPS
the Protected Users group
Group Managed Service Account (gMSA)
Windows LAPS-managed local account
Protected Users group membership
Just Enough Administration (JEA) endpoint

madlibs.explanation: JEA defines constrained PowerShell endpoints that expose only an approved set of cmdlets to a role, without handing out full administrative rights — exactly the narrowly scoped access described. A gMSA is the account type purpose-built for automatic, complex password management on service accounts; Windows LAPS instead manages local administrator account passwords (not service accounts), and Protected Users restricts authentication protocols rather than managing any password.

sequences.prompt: Put these steps in order for promoting a new Windows Server to be an additional domain controller in an existing AD DS domain.
steps: Install the Active Directory Domain Services role
Run the AD DS configuration wizard and choose 'Add a domain controller to an existing domain'
Specify the domain and supply credentials with sufficient privilege
Configure DNS and Global Catalog options
Complete the promotion and reboot the server
sequences.explanation: The role has to be installed before the configuration wizard exists to run at all — and the wizard needs the target domain and privileged credentials before it can present DNS/Global Catalog options, since those options depend on knowing which domain you're joining.

sequences.prompt: Put these steps in order for setting up hybrid identity sync between on-premises AD DS and Microsoft Entra ID.
steps: Prepare on-premises AD DS (clean up duplicate/invalid attributes)
Install Microsoft Entra Connect on a member server
Configure sync rules and select which OUs to sync
Verify users and groups appear correctly in Microsoft Entra ID
sequences.explanation: Skipping AD cleanup is the single most common real-world cause of sync errors, so it has to happen first. Sync rules/OU scope must be configured before the initial sync runs, or the first sync pushes the wrong (or everything) up to Entra ID.

sequences.prompt: Put these steps in order for setting up a highly available file server using Windows Failover Clustering.
steps: Install the Failover Clustering feature on each node
Add shared storage to the cluster
Configure the File Server role as a clustered role
sequences.explanation: Cluster validation runs against nodes that already have the feature installed, and has to pass before creating the cluster is fully supported. The File Server role can't be configured as clustered until the cluster and its shared storage both already exist.

caseStudies.title: Fabrikam Manufacturing's Hybrid Infrastructure Refresh
caseStudies.scenario: Fabrikam Manufacturing runs a single Active Directory forest, fabrikam.local, with domain controllers at its main plant and at two branch offices connected back to the plant by slow, metered WAN links. Fabrikam wants Microsoft Entra ID sign-in for its cloud apps to keep working even during a brief on-premises AD outage, without standing up and maintaining AD FS servers. Separately, the IT team is retiring an aging physical file server by virtualizing it as a Hyper-V VM, and that VM's file share must become highly available through Windows Failover Clustering with shared storage, while a second, asynchronously updated copy of the same VM is kept at a disaster-recovery site in case the primary plant is lost entirely. Finally, an audit flagged that local administrator passwords on Fabrikam's servers are identical across many machines, and the security team wants every server to get its own unique, automatically rotated local admin password with no one ever needing to manually set or remember it.

questions.question: Which Microsoft Entra Connect authentication method should Fabrikam choose so that cloud sign-in keeps working through a brief on-premises AD outage, without deploying AD FS?
options: Password Hash Synchronization
Pass-through Authentication
Federation with AD FS
Seamless SSO used on its own with no other method
questions.explanation: Password Hash Synchronization lets Microsoft Entra ID validate sign-ins on its own using a synchronized hash, so authentication keeps working even if on-premises AD is briefly unreachable. Pass-through Authentication and Federation both depend on validating against on-premises infrastructure at the moment of sign-in, so both fail during that same outage — and Seamless SSO by itself isn't an authentication method, it only removes extra sign-in prompts on top of one.

questions.question: True or false: because the branch offices are connected to the main plant by slow WAN links, replication between those sites uses the same near-real-time change notification that domain controllers within the same site use.
questions.explanation: Inter-site replication is deliberately scheduled and compressed to be considerate of limited WAN bandwidth, unlike intra-site replication, which does use change notification for near-immediate convergence. The slow links are exactly why Fabrikam's branch-to-plant replication behaves differently from replication within a single site, not the same way.

questions.question: Which two of the following are steps in building the highly available clustered file server itself, as opposed to the separate disaster-recovery copy? (Select two.)
options: Install the Failover Clustering feature on each node
Configure Hyper-V Replica to the disaster-recovery site
Validate the cluster configuration before creating the cluster
Enable Windows LAPS on the file server VM
questions.explanation: Installing Failover Clustering and validating the cluster configuration are both required steps toward creating the highly available cluster itself. Hyper-V Replica is the separate, unrelated mechanism that produces the asynchronous DR copy at the secondary site, and Windows LAPS manages local admin passwords — neither one builds or validates the cluster.
questions.whyTested: Case studies deliberately bundle a DR requirement and an HA requirement into the same scenario so a candidate has to sort which stated steps satisfy which requirement, rather than treating every clustering-adjacent term as interchangeable — Hyper-V Replica and Failover Clustering solve two different problems even though both appear in the same VM's story.

questions.question: Which capability directly addresses the audit finding, giving every server its own unique, automatically rotated local administrator password with no one needing to manually set or remember it?
options: Windows LAPS
Group Managed Service Account (gMSA)
Just Enough Administration (JEA)
Protected Users group membership
questions.explanation: Windows LAPS is built specifically to randomize and automatically rotate the built-in local administrator account's password on each managed machine, backing it up to AD DS or Microsoft Entra ID. A gMSA solves the equivalent problem for a service account's password, not a local admin account; JEA scopes what cmdlets an admin can run rather than managing any password; and Protected Users only restricts which authentication protocols an account can fall back to.
